# Overview


This page introduces the **H4 tail benchmarking** repository: what problem it solves, how its pieces fit together, and where a new developer should go next. It covers the repository's purpose, the underlying MD-to-SAXS comparison workflow, the layout of files and folders, and a guided reading path through the rest of this documentation. It intentionally stays at the conceptual level — implementation details live in the Deep Dive pages linked throughout.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L9)

## What This Repository Does

This repository provides tools to **compare intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) structural ensembles generated from molecular dynamics (MD) against small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) experimental data**. IDPs like the H4 histone tail do not adopt a single folded structure — they exist as a *cloud* of conformations. SAXS experiments probe that cloud as an ensemble average, but raw SAXS data alone cannot tell you *which* conformations are present. This repository bridges the two worlds: it takes an MD-generated conformational pool, refines it against SAXS data using the Ensemble Optimization Method (EOM), and quantifies how much the SAXS-consistent sub-ensemble differs from the full MD ensemble.

The working example throughout is the **H4 histone tail** — a 26-residue, fully disordered protein segment — from the paper: *Tong Wang, Egor S. Kolesnikov, Lois Pollack, Alexey V. Onufriev. "Combining atomistic simulation and solution scattering to reveal charge-driven histone H4 tail conformational changes" (2026, in submission)*. If you use this code, the README asks you to cite that paper. The project is licensed under Apache 2.0.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L9), [README.md](README.md#L27-L28)

## The Core Idea: One Pipeline, Two Comparisons

The scientific workflow has two halves. The **half you cannot run from this repo alone** is the EOM suite from the external ATSAS package: **RANCH** generates random conformations, **FFMAKER** computes theoretical SAXS profiles for each, and **GAJOE** uses a genetic algorithm (backed by CRYSOL) to select the sub-ensemble of conformations whose averaged profile best fits the experimental SAXS curve. The **half this repository owns** is everything *after* GAJOE: reconstructing which conformations the genetic algorithm kept, visualizing full-pool vs. selected-ensemble distributions, and computing the **Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD)** — an information-theoretic measure of how different two probability distributions are — between the MD ensemble and the SAXS-refined ensemble.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph External["ATSAS tools (external install)"]
        A[Conformational pool<br/>from MD e.g. AMBER,<br/>or RANCH-generated] --> B[FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles<br/>+ size statistics]
        B --> C[GAJOE<br/>genetic algorithm<br/>ensemble fitting]
    end
    D[(Experimental SAXS<br/>SAXSData/*.dat)] --> C
    C --> E[(GAJOE output folder<br/>GA001/curve_1/)]
    subgraph Repo["This repository"]
        E --> F[getBestCurve.m<br/>reconstruct selected<br/>conformation counts]
        F --> G[make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>2D histograms +<br/>Jensen-Shannon divergence]
        E --> H[plotEOMSAXScomparison.m<br/>SAXS fit, Kratky plot,<br/>residuals]
        E --> I[Python: graph.py / 2d.py<br/>quick plots from tutorial]
    end
    G --> J((Quantified ensemble<br/>shift: MD vs SAXS))
    H --> J
```

Reading the diagram left to right: conformations enter from MD or RANCH, get converted to theoretical scattering by FFMAKER, and GAJOE optimizes a sub-ensemble against the experimental curve. Everything downstream of the GAJOE output folder is what this repository ships code for.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L17), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L206), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L4-L16)

## Repository Layout at a Glance

The repository is deliberately flat — three MATLAB scripts at the root, and three folders of supporting data. Nothing needs to be built or compiled; the scripts are run directly against the data folders.

```
H4_tail_benchmarking/
├── getBestCurve.m                  ← helper: reconstructs GA-selected structure counts
├── make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m     ← 2D histograms + Jensen-Shannon divergence
├── plotEOMSAXScomparison.m         ← SAXS fit, Kratky plot, residuals
├── ExampleData/
│   └── H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/
│       └── GA001/curve_1/          ← full example GAJOE output (100 GA cycles)
├── SAXSData/
│   ├── H4WT_150Na.dat              ← experimental SAXS: wild-type H4 tail
│   └── H4KQ_150Na.dat              ← experimental SAXS: K→Q (charge-neutralized) H4
├── Example_tutorial/               ← self-contained 20-conformation EOM demo
└── LICENSE.txt
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L17)

| Path | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `getBestCurve.m` | MATLAB function | Parses `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files across all GA runs and counts how often each conformation was selected |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | MATLAB script | Builds Rg–Ree and Dmax–Rg 2D scatter/histogram figures for full pool vs. EOM ensemble; computes JSD for Rg and Ree |
| `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | MATLAB script | Plots experimental SAXS vs. EOM ensemble fit, a dimensionless Kratky plot, and fit residuals |
| `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/` | GAJOE output | Complete worked example: 100 `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files, `Rg_distr_001_1.txt`, `Size_distr_001_1.txt`, `CaCa_distr_001_1.txt`, `Volume_distr_001_1.txt`, `Size_list.txt`, `Ree_values.mat`, `profiles_001_1.fit` |
| `SAXSData/` | Experimental data | Two measured SAXS profiles: wild-type H4 and K-to-Q mutant at 150 mM Na |
| `Example_tutorial/` | Tutorial workspace | Minimal 20-conformation EOM run: RANCH inputs (`assignment.txt`, `protein.seq`), experimental data, and two Python plotting scripts |

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L2-L9), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L39), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L16), [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3)

> [!TIP]
> GAJOE v2.x **no longer writes a `best_curve.txt` file** (v1.3 did). The `getBestCurve.m` function exists precisely to reconstruct it from the `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` workfiles — but this only works if you answered **yes** to "Save workfiles with the entire GA runs?" during the GAJOE run. If you skip that prompt, the MATLAB analysis cannot recover which conformations were selected.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L3-L9)

## The Analysis Scripts: One Entry Point Each

Both main MATLAB scripts follow the same beginner-friendly pattern: a **"User-defined parameters" block at the top of the file** where you set paths and options, then run the whole script. As the README puts it, "mostly the paths just need to be matched."

| Script | Key inputs you configure | What you get out |
|---|---|---|
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | GAJOE output `dir`, `nRuns` (GA repetitions, e.g. 100), `curvesPerEnsemble` (e.g. 20), axis limits, histogram bins | Two publication-quality figures (Rg vs. Ree; Dmax vs. Rg) with marginal histograms, printed mean/standard-error statistics, and JSD values quantifying MD-vs-EOM distribution differences |
| `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | GAJOE output `folder`, experimental `.dat` file, plot color, axis limits | Three panels: linear I(q) fit overlay, dimensionless Kratky plot, and interpolated residuals (I_exp − I_theor) |
| `getBestCurve.m` | Called by the 2D script: `dir`, `nRuns`, `curvesPerEnsemble` | A two-column matrix `[conformation index, selection frequency]` — the reconstructed "best curve" |
| `graph.py` (tutorial) | `folder` path to GAJOE output | `saxs_fit.png`, `rg.png`, `dmax.png`, `ree.png` |
| `2d.py` (tutorial) | `size_file` + `selected_dir` (GAJOE's `pdbs/`) | Rg–Ree scatter with marginal histograms highlighting GAJOE-selected conformations |

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L27), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L22), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L2-L4), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L59), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L41)

## What the Example Data Shows

The bundled `ExampleData` folder is a real GAJOE run against the wild-type H4 tail. Inside `GA001/curve_1/`, each `GA_CYCLE_N.txt` file is one independent genetic algorithm run — the log format shows generation number, best chi², and the dash-delimited list of selected conformation indices (e.g. `-122-180-257-...`). The distribution files (`Rg_distr`, `Size_distr`, `CaCa_distr`, `Volume_distr`) contain radius of gyration, maximum dimension, end-to-end distance, and volume distributions for both the full pool and the selected ensemble, while `profiles_001_1.fit` holds the experimental-vs-fitted scattering curve including χ². The companion `SAXSData/` folder holds the two experimental curves (WT and K-to-Q) that drive the charge-driven conformational-change story of the paper.

Sources: [GA_CYCLE_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_1.txt#L1-L15), [README.md](README.md#L12-L13), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16)

The `Example_tutorial/` folder is a **self-contained miniature of the whole pipeline**: `protein.seq` defines the 26-residue H4 sequence (`SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`), and `assignment.txt` tells RANCH to treat residue range 1–26 as `disordered`. The README documents a four-command walkthrough — `ranch`, `ffmaker`, `gajoe`, then two Python scripts — that takes you from sequence to final plots in minutes, using only 20 conformations.

> [!TIP]
> The 20-conformation tutorial pool exists **only to demonstrate the workflow mechanics**, as the README explicitly warns. For quantitative science, you need a substantially larger, well-sampled conformational pool, more GA generations, and more independent GA runs.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3), [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [README.md](README.md#L89-L118)

## Hardware and Software Requirements

The analysis is deliberately lightweight: a standard computer with enough memory for "moderate intensity computing tasks" is sufficient, because the heavy lifting (MD simulation, CRYSOL profile calculation) happens in external tools. The external dependencies are: **ATSAS** (specifically GAJOE v2.1 recommended), **AMBER 24** (only if you generate your own MD ensembles), and **MATLAB R2021 or later**. The Python plotting scripts additionally need `numpy` and `matplotlib`.

| Dependency | Version | Needed for |
|---|---|---|
| ATSAS (RANCH, FFMAKER, GAJOE) | GAJOE v2.1 recommended | Pool generation, profile calculation, GA fitting |
| MATLAB | R2021+ | All three root analysis scripts |
| Python | numpy, matplotlib | Tutorial plots (`graph.py`, `2d.py`) |
| AMBER 24 | — | Only for generating new MD ensembles |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L25), [README.md](README.md#L102-L106)

## Suggested Reading Path

This documentation follows a Get Started → Deep Dive progression. A recommended route for a new developer:

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — get the example data running end-to-end with minimal setup.
2. **[Software Requirements and Installation](3-software-requirements-and-installation)** — install ATSAS, MATLAB, and Python dependencies properly.
3. **[EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools)** — run the 20-conformation walkthrough yourself.
4. **[Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview)** — then understand *why* the pieces are shaped this way.
5. Follow the *EOM Pipeline Concepts* track ([RANCH](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation) → [FFMAKER](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles) → [GAJOE](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) → [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference)) to master the external toolchain.
6. Finish with the *MATLAB Analysis Scripts* and *Python Plotting Utilities* tracks — starting with [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles) and [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification), which contain the repository's core scientific contribution.
7. For the biology behind it all, read the [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study), then see how to generalize in [Extending Workflow to Other IDPs](19-extending-workflow-to-other-idps).


# Quick Start



This page gets you from a fresh clone to your first EOM result in two independent paths: **Path A** runs the complete ATSAS pipeline (RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE → Python plots) on a small 20-conformation H4 histone tail demo shipped in `Example_tutorial/`, and **Path B** analyzes the pre-computed GAJOE output in `ExampleData/` using the repository's MATLAB scripts — no ATSAS installation required. The repository's core purpose is comparing intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) structural ensembles generated from molecular dynamics (MD) against small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data, with the H4 histone tail as the worked example case.

![H4 SAXS MD benchmarking overview graphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L17), [README.md](README.md#L3)

## What You Need Before Starting

The analysis runs on a standard computer with enough memory for moderate computing tasks — no workstation or GPU cluster is needed for the Quick Start demo. The toolchain divides into a mandatory core (ATSAS + Python) and an optional MATLAB layer used only for Path B and the deeper ensemble analysis described in the Deep Dive pages.

| Component | Role in Quick Start | Version note | Needed for |
|---|---|---|---|
| ATSAS (RANCH, FFMAKER, GAJOE) | Generates conformers, theoretical SAXS profiles, ensemble fits | GAJOE v2.1 is easiest | Path A, Steps 1–4 |
| Python + `numpy` + `matplotlib` | Plots SAXS fit and Rg–Ree scatter | Any recent 3.x | Path A, Step 5 |
| MATLAB | 2D histograms, SAXS fit/Kratky/residual comparison | R2021 or later | Path B (optional) |
| AMBER 24 | MD ensemble generation | 24 | Not needed on this page |

If you have not yet installed ATSAS, follow [Software Requirements and Installation](3-software-requirements-and-installation) first — the ATSAS download is at https://www.embl-hamburg.de/biosaxs/software.html.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L25), [README.md](README.md#L34)

## A Map of the Repository

Only four locations matter for the Quick Start, and each maps to exactly one stage of the workflow.

```
H4_tail_benchmarking/
├── Example_tutorial/          ← Path A workspace: a complete, self-contained demo
│   ├── protein.seq            ← H4 tail sequence fed to RANCH
│   ├── assignment.txt         ← RANCH domain assignment
│   ├── H4WT_150Na.dat         ← experimental SAXS data (fit target)
│   ├── graph.py / 2d.py       ← Python plotting scripts
│   └── keeper.git
├── ExampleData/
│   └── H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/   ← Path B: pre-computed GAJOE output
├── SAXSData/
│   ├── H4WT_150Na.dat         ← wild-type experimental profile
│   └── H4KQ_150Na.dat         ← charge-neutralized (K→Q) profile
├── getBestCurve.m             ← rebuilds GAJOE v2 best-curve from GA cycles
├── make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m ← 2D histogram: MD pool vs SAXS-refined ensemble
└── plotEOMSAXScomparison.m    ← averaged EOM SAXS profile vs experiment
```

| Path | Quick Start role |
|---|---|
| `Example_tutorial/` | Self-contained 20-conformer EOM demo; run all four ATSAS stages here |
| `ExampleData/.../GA001/curve_1/` | Shipped GAJOE results: `profiles_001_1.fit`, 100 `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files, `Rg_distr`, `Size_distr`, `CaCa_distr` distributions, `Size_list.txt`, `Ree_values.mat` |
| `SAXSData/` | Experimental SAXS profiles (53 q-points, format: `Q  I(Q)  Error` after 4 header lines) |
| Three `.m` scripts at root | Post-GAJOE MATLAB analysis layer |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L17), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L5)

## How the Pieces Fit Together

The pipeline is a strictly linear chain of three ATSAS programs, with two visualization front-ends branching off the GAJOE output. Understanding this shape before typing any commands makes every subsequent step self-explanatory: each tool consumes the previous tool's file and emits files whose names the next stage expects.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph IN["Inputs"]
        SEQ["protein.seq + assignment.txt<br/>(26-residue H4 tail)"]
        EXP["H4WT_150Na.dat<br/>(experimental SAXS)"]
    end
    subgraph ATSAS["ATSAS pipeline"]
        R["RANCH<br/>random conformational pool<br/>→ 20 CIF models"]
        F["FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles<br/>intensities_20.csv + size_statistics_20.csv"]
        G["GAJOE<br/>genetic-algorithm<br/>ensemble selection"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["GAJOE output: GA001/"]
        FIT["profiles_*.fit"]
        DIST["Rg / Dmax / Ree distributions"]
        PDBS["pdbs/ selected conformers"]
    end
    subgraph VIZ["Visualization"]
        PY["graph.py + 2d.py (Python)"]
        ML["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>plotEOMSAXScomparison.m (MATLAB)"]
    end
    SEQ --> R --> F --> G
    EXP --> G
    G --> FIT & DIST & PDBS
    FIT & DIST & PDBS --> PY
    OUT --> ML
```

Note that GAJOE is the only stage that touches the experimental data — RANCH and FFMAKER work purely on the model side, which is why Path B can analyze pre-computed GAJOE output without regenerating anything upstream.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L17), [README.md](README.md#L38-L98)

## Path A — Your First EOM Run in `Example_tutorial`

This is the complete hands-on sequence. The demo deliberately uses a tiny 20-conformation pool and modest GA settings so the whole cycle finishes quickly; a full quantitative analysis scales these up later.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Install ATSAS + numpy/matplotlib"] --> B["cd Example_tutorial"]
    B --> C["Step 1: RANCH<br/>mkdir pool_20 && ranch ...<br/>→ pool_20/ with 20 CIF models"]
    C --> D["Step 2: FFMAKER<br/>→ intensities_20.csv<br/>→ size_statistics_20.csv"]
    D --> E["Step 3: GAJOE<br/>fit against H4WT_150Na.dat<br/>→ GA001/"]
    E --> F["Step 4: edit paths in graph.py and 2d.py"]
    F --> G["python graph.py<br/>→ saxs_fit.png, rg.png, dmax.png, ree.png"]
    G --> H["python 2d.py<br/>→ EOM_2D.png"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [README.md](README.md#L38-L118)

### Step 1 — Install and Enter the Workspace

After installing ATSAS, install the two Python dependencies and change into the tutorial directory. Everything you need is already there: the experimental dataset `H4WT_150Na.dat`, 20 example PDB structures, the two plotting scripts, and the two RANCH input files described in the next step.

```bash
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib
cd Example_tutorial
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L34-L36), [README.md](README.md#L102-L106)

### Step 2 — Generate Conformations with RANCH

RANCH builds a random conformational pool from two text inputs. `assignment.txt` declares a single residue range as disordered (`A 1 26 disordered`), and `protein.seq` carries the 26-residue H4 tail sequence `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`. The `--seed` flag makes the random pool reproducible.

```bash
mkdir pool_20

ranch --repetitions 20 --prefix pool_20/model_ \
    --seed 12345 assignment.txt protein.seq
```

**Output:** a `pool_20/` directory containing 20 randomly generated conformations in CIF format.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L47), [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2)

### Step 3 — Compute Theoretical SAXS Profiles with FFMAKER

FFMAKER converts every CIF model into a theoretical intensity profile and a size-statistics table. Both outputs are the mandatory inputs to GAJOE in the next step.

```bash
ffmaker --output intensities_20.csv \
    --pool size_statistics_20.csv pool_20/*.cif
```

| Output file | Contents |
|---|---|
| `intensities_20.csv` | Theoretical SAXS intensity profiles for all 20 conformations |
| `size_statistics_20.csv` | Per-conformation structural properties: R_g, D_max, end-to-end distance (R_ee), and volume |

To analyze the provided PDB structures instead of a fresh RANCH pool, replace `pool_20/*.cif` with the path to those PDB files.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L49-L60)

### Step 4 — Fit Ensembles with GAJOE

GAJOE runs a genetic algorithm that selects the subset of conformers whose averaged theoretical profile best matches the experimental data. The command line encodes every major fitting decision:

```bash
gajoe \
    --intensity intensities_20.csv \
    --size size_statistics_20.csv \
    --times 1 \
    --generation 100 \
    --ensemble 20 \
    --minimum 1 \
    --maximum 10 \
    --no-repeated \
    H4WT_150Na.dat
```

| Flag | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--intensity` | `intensities_20.csv` | Theoretical SAXS profiles from FFMAKER |
| `--size` | `size_statistics_20.csv` | Structural properties (R_g, D_max, R_ee) per conformer |
| `--times` | `1` | Number of independent genetic algorithm runs |
| `--generation` | `100` | Generations per run |
| `--ensemble` | `20` | Candidate ensembles evaluated per generation |
| `--minimum` / `--maximum` | `1` / `10` | Bounds on conformations in the selected ensemble |
| `--no-repeated` | — | Prevents the same conformer appearing twice within one ensemble |
| *(positional)* | `H4WT_150Na.dat` | Experimental SAXS data to fit |

**Output:** a `GA001/` directory containing `profiles_*.fit` (experimental data plus fitted ensemble intensity with χ²), `Rg_distr_*.txt`, `Size_distr_*.txt`, and `CaCa_distr_*.txt` distribution files, a `pdbs/` subfolder with the selected conformations, and `logFile_*.log` with all optimization settings. The full file anatomy is documented in [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference).

These settings are intended for a quick demonstration only — for quantitative analysis, increase generations and independent runs, and use a substantially larger conformational pool.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L62-L98)

### Step 5 — Plot with the Python Scripts

Both scripts hard-code their input paths near the top, so the only edit required is pointing them at your fresh GAJOE output directory before running them.

| Script | Edit this line | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| `graph.py` | `folder = Path("GA001/curve_1")` | `saxs_fit.png` (experiment + GAJOE fit, log-scale I(q)); `rg.png`, `dmax.png`, `ree.png` distribution overlays |
| `2d.py` | `size_file = Path("size_statistics_20.csv")` and `selected_dir = Path("GA001/curve_1/pdbs")` | `EOM_2D.png` — R_g vs R_ee scatter of the full pool with GAJOE-selected conformers circled, plus marginal histograms |

```bash
python graph.py
python 2d.py
```

`2d.py` cross-checks the selected conformers against the pool statistics and prints a summary (`Pool: N`, `Selected by GAJOE: N`) before rendering, failing loudly with an assertion if any selected structure is missing from the pool.

> [!TIP]
> `graph.py` silently skips a distribution plot when no file matches its glob (`if not files: continue`), and its patterns expect `Rg_distr_*.dat` / `Size_distr_*.dat` / `CaCa_distr_*.dat` — yet GAJOE commonly writes these as `.txt` files (exactly what the shipped `ExampleData` contains). If only `saxs_fit.png` appears, rename the distribution files or relax the glob patterns.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L118), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L5), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L59), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L9), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L36-L41), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L106)

## Path B — Zero-Install Analysis of the Shipped Example Data

The repository ships a complete, pre-computed GAJOE run (`ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/`, 100 GA cycles) alongside the experimental profiles, so the two MATLAB scripts work immediately after cloning — both already have repo-relative paths configured in their **User-defined parameters** block, which the README notes is the only block you ever interact with. This is also how the published H4WT figure was produced.

| Script | Parameter | Value in repo | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | `folder` | `ExampleData/.../GA001/curve_1` | GAJOE output directory |
| | `expData` | `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat`, `NumHeaderLines=4` | Experimental profile (Q, I(Q), Error columns) |
| | `fitFile` | `profiles_001_1.fit`, `NumHeaderLines=1` | GAJOE fitted profile |
| | `theColour` | `[238 68 0]/255` (H4WT) or `[46 80 122]/255` (H4KQ) | Plot color per variant |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | `dir` | `ExampleData/.../GA001/curve_1` | GAJOE output directory |
| | `nRuns` | `100` | Number of GA runs — must match your GAJOE `--times` setting |
| | `curvesPerEnsemble` | `20` | Maximum curves per ensemble |

Running `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` produces the SAXS-vs-EOM overlay, a Kratky representation, and residual plots; `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` produces the 2D (R_g, R_ee) histogram comparison between the full MD pool and the SAXS-refined ensemble, including the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the two distributions. Both scripts route through the helper `getBestCurve.m`, which exists because GAJOE v2 dropped the `best_curve.txt` file of v1.3 — it reconstructs the selected-structure frequencies by tallying structures across all `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files and returns a `[PDB_number, frequency]` matrix. For `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` specifically, the shipped dataset already contains the required `Ree_values.mat` and `Size_list.txt`, so no pre-processing is needed on your side.

> [!TIP]
> `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files — the raw material `getBestCurve.m` reads — are only written when you answer `y` to GAJOE's prompt *"Save workfiles with the entire GA runs? (default: no)"*. If you run your own GAJOE job intending to use the MATLAB scripts later, make sure this option is enabled, or `getBestCurve` will have nothing to read.

The K→Q (charge-neutralized) comparison uses the same scripts — swap `expData` to `SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat` and the color to the blue variant. The scientific interpretation of these two variants is covered in [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study), and the divergence metric itself in [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L17), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L31), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L55), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L22), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L2-L11), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L19-L39)

## Where to Go Next

If anything in this page raised questions about *why* the pipeline is shaped this way, the conceptual grounding lives in [Overview](1-overview) and [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview). Practical follow-ups in reading order:

1. **[Software Requirements and Installation](3-software-requirements-and-installation)** — if ATSAS or MATLAB are not yet installed, resolve this before running Path A.
2. **[EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools)** — the step-by-step ATSAS walkthrough this page summarized, with deeper command context.
3. **Python plotting deep dives** — [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots) extends `graph.py`, and [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals) extends `2d.py`.
4. **Scaling up** — [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation), [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles), and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) explain how to grow the 20-conformer demo into a production-grade analysis.

The repository is released under the Apache 2.0 License; if you use the code in published work, cite the accompanying paper (Wang, Kolesnikov, Pollack, Onufriev, 2026, in submission).


# Software Requirements and Installation



This page specifies everything you need to install before running the H4 tail benchmarking workflow, which compares intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) ensembles from molecular dynamics (MD) against small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data. The workflow has three mandatory software components — the **ATSAS suite**, **MATLAB**, and a small **Python environment** — plus one optional dependency, **AMBER**, that you only need if you plan to generate your own MD ensembles. By the end of this page you will know exactly what to install, which versions matter, how each component fits into the pipeline, and how to verify your setup end-to-end.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L8), [README.md](README.md#L22-L25)

## The Software Stack at a Glance

The repository splits its work across four environments. **ATSAS** (developed and distributed by EMBL Hamburg) performs the Ensemble Optimization Method (EOM) pipeline: RANCH builds random conformational pools, FFMAKER computes theoretical SAXS profiles, and GAJOE fits ensembles to experimental data using a genetic algorithm. **MATLAB** scripts then compare the full MD ensemble with the SAXS-refined ensemble and plot the fit against experiment. **Python** scripts provide lightweight plotting for the bundled tutorial, and **AMBER** is only involved upstream when producing MD ensembles from scratch.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Core["ATSAS Suite — EMBL Hamburg (REQUIRED)"]
        RANCH["RANCH<br/>conformational pool generation"]
        FFMAKER["FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles"]
        GAJOE["GAJOE (v2.1 recommended)<br/>GA ensemble fitting"]
    end
    subgraph ML["MATLAB R2021+ (REQUIRED for analysis scripts)"]
        GBC["getBestCurve.m"]
        M2D["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m"]
        PEOM["plotEOMSAXScomparison.m"]
    end
    subgraph PY["Python 3 + numpy + matplotlib (REQUIRED for tutorial plots)"]
        G["graph.py"]
        D2["2d.py"]
    end
    subgraph OPT["Optional"]
        AMBER["AMBER 24<br/>MD ensemble generation"]
    end
    RANCH --> FFMAKER --> GAJOE
    GAJOE -->|"GA001 output folder"| GBC
    GBC --> M2D
    GAJOE --> PEOM
    GAJOE -->|"profiles, distributions"| G
    GAJOE -->|"size stats, selected pdbs"| D2
    AMBER -.->|"custom ensembles only"| RANCH
```

| Component | Role in the Workflow | Version Guidance | Required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| ATSAS (RANCH, FFMAKER, GAJOE) | EOM pipeline: pool generation, SAXS profile calculation, GA fitting | GAJOE v2.1 recommended ("will be easiest") | **Required** |
| MATLAB | 2D ensemble histograms, Jensen-Shannon divergence, SAXS fit/Kratky/residual plots | R2021 or later | **Required** for the MATLAB analysis scripts |
| Python 3 + numpy + matplotlib | Tutorial SAXS curve, Rg–Ree scatter with marginals | Any modern Python 3 (no version pinned) | **Required** to reproduce the tutorial plots |
| AMBER 24 | Generating MD structural ensembles (ff19SB/OPC path) | AMBER 24 used in the paper | **Optional** — example GAJOE results ship in `ExampleData/` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L13), [README.md](README.md#L19-L25), [Example_tutorial/2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L2-L4), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L7-L8)

## Hardware Requirements

No exotic hardware is needed. The authors state the analysis "should only require a standard computer that is able to run the commonly available software below, with enough memory to complete moderate intensity computing tasks." In practice, your machine mainly needs to be able to run MATLAB and ATSAS comfortably; the heavy lifting (MD simulation) is only relevant if you opt into the AMBER path.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L20)

## Installing ATSAS (Core Dependency)

ATSAS is the backbone of the entire workflow — EOM and GAJOE are part of it, and the repository explicitly recommends **GAJOE v2.1** as the easiest version to use. Obtain ATSAS from the EMBL Hamburg download page linked in the repository's tutorial, complete their registration, and install it so the command-line tools (`ranch`, `ffmaker`, `gajoe`) are on your `PATH`. The repository's tutorial then drives these tools purely from the terminal, so a working CLI is the verification target — no GUI configuration is required by this project.

The three commands you must be able to call are exactly those exercised in the tutorial: `ranch` (generate conformations), `ffmaker` (theoretical SAXS profiles + size statistics), and `gajoe` (genetic-algorithm ensemble fitting against an experimental `.dat` file). If any of them responds with "command not found," add your ATSAS installation's binary directory to your `PATH` before proceeding.

> [!TIP]
> Version sensitivity matters here: the MATLAB scripts in this repository were "adapted for use with GAJOE v2.1," which **no longer outputs a `best_curve.txt` file** (that was a v1.3 feature). Installing GAJOE v2.x keeps the pipeline consistent with `getBestCurve.m`, which programmatically rebuilds the missing best-curve data from GA cycle files.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11), [README.md](README.md#L22-L23), [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L6-L8)

## MATLAB Environment

The three analysis scripts require **MATLAB R2021 or later** per the repository's software notes. Examining the scripts confirms why a recent release matters: `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` and `getBestCurve.m` both rely on `readmatrix` (introduced in R2019a), including its text-file options, and the plots use the LaTeX text interpreter for axis labels. One script also depends on a toolbox function, which is the single most commonly missed installation step for beginners — detailed in the table below.

| Script | Key MATLAB Functions Used | Installation Note |
|---|---|---|
| `getBestCurve.m` | `readmatrix`, `categorical`, `tabulate` | `tabulate` belongs to the **Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox** — verify it is included in your MATLAB license |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | `importdata`, `load`, `repmat`, LaTeX interpreter | Base MATLAB; R2021+ recommended by the README |
| `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | `readmatrix` with `'FileType','text'`, `interp1` | `readmatrix` requires R2019a+ |

Both high-level scripts are run by editing the "User-defined parameters" block at the top — mostly path matching to your GAJOE output folder — so no additional MATLAB configuration is needed beyond the installation itself.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L25), [README.md](README.md#L17), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L20-L30), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L18), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L73-L74)

## Python Environment

The Python footprint is deliberately minimal — exactly **two third-party packages**. The repository gives the exact install command in its tutorial, and inspection of both scripts confirms nothing beyond `numpy`, `matplotlib` (including `GridSpec` for the marginal-histogram layout), and the standard-library `pathlib` is imported. Any standard Python 3 environment works; there is no pinned version, no `requirements.txt`, and no conda file in the repository.

```bash
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib
```

| Package | Imported By | Role | Source of Truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| `numpy` | `graph.py`, `2d.py` | Array math for SAXS curves, Rg/Ree statistics | First import line of each script |
| `matplotlib` (pyplot, GridSpec) | `graph.py`, `2d.py` | SAXS fit plots, distribution plots, 2D scatter with marginals | Import lines + `GridSpec` usage |
| `pathlib` (stdlib) | `graph.py`, `2d.py` | Locating GAJOE output files via glob patterns | Built into Python 3 — nothing to install |

The scripts are then run directly with no arguments: `python graph.py` produces the experimental SAXS curve and EOM fit, and `python 2d.py` produces the Rg-versus-Ree scatter plot with marginal histograms (after you point each script's folder variable at your GAJOE output directory).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L116), [Example_tutorial/graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L1-L5), [Example_tutorial/2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L2-L9)

## AMBER 24 (Optional — MD Ensemble Generation)

AMBER is listed in the software notes because the paper's H4 tail ensembles were produced with **AMBER 24**, but it sits outside the analysis pipeline itself. If you only want to benchmark existing ensembles against SAXS data, skip this entirely — the repository ships example GAJOE results (`ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/`) and both wild-type and K-to-Q experimental SAXS profiles (`SAXSData/`), so the full MATLAB analysis path runs without any MD software installed. If you do intend to generate your own ensembles, install AMBER 24 and continue to the dedicated MD page afterward.

> [!TIP]
> Check the `ExampleData` folder name: `H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC` records the force field (ff19SB) and water model (OPC) used for the shipped ensemble — useful context if you later install AMBER to reproduce or extend the MD side, but irrelevant to the ATSAS/MATLAB/Python installation on this page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L13), [README.md](README.md#L24)

## Verifying Your Setup (End-to-End Smoke Test)

The fastest confidence check is to run the bundled tutorial in `Example_tutorial/`, which contains everything needed: an experimental SAXS dataset (`H4WT_150Na.dat`), 20 example PDB structures, the two Python plotting scripts, and the two RANCH input files (`assignment.txt`, `protein.seq`). The following sequence exercises every component you just installed — ATSAS three times, Python once — and finishes in minutes on a standard computer:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Start: environment installed"] --> A["1. Verify ATSAS CLIs:<br/>ranch, ffmaker, gajoe respond to --help"]
    A -->|"command not found"| A1["Add ATSAS bin directory to PATH"]
    A1 --> A
    A -->|"OK"| B["2. RANCH: generate 20-conformation pool<br/>mkdir pool_20 + ranch command"]
    B --> C["3. FFMAKER: intensities_20.csv<br/>+ size_statistics_20.csv"]
    C --> D["4. GAJOE: fit H4WT_150Na.dat<br/>produces GA001/ folder"]
    D --> E["5. Python: set folder in graph.py / 2d.py"]
    E --> F{"saxs_fit.png and<br/>EOM_2D.png generated?"}
    F -->|"Yes"| G["✅ Environment verified"]
    F -->|"No"| T["Check Troubleshooting table below"]
```

A successful run confirms ATSAS end-to-end: GAJOE writes a `GA001`-style directory containing `profiles_*.fit`, the `Rg_distr_*.txt` / `Size_distr_*.txt` / `CaCa_distr_*.txt` distributions, a `pdbs/` folder of selected conformations, and a `logFile_*.log` — precisely the files the MATLAB and Python scripts consume next. Note that the tutorial's small 20-conformation pool is explicitly a workflow demonstration; quantitative analysis later requires much larger pools, but the 20-structure smoke test is ideal for installation verification.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [README.md](README.md#L38-L75), [README.md](README.md#L91-L98), [README.md](README.md#L108-L118)

## What the Repository Provides

No data acquisition is needed to get started — the repository bundles the example GAJOE output folder (`ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/`), experimental SAXS profiles for wild-type and charge-neutralized (K-to-Q) H4 tails in `SAXSData/`, three MATLAB analysis scripts at the root, and the complete self-contained tutorial directory. This means the **minimum viable installation** for exploring the project is ATSAS + MATLAB (for the root scripts) or just ATSAS + Python (for the tutorial):

```
H4_tail_benchmarking/
├── ExampleData/
│   └── H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/
│       └── GA001/                  ← example GAJOE output (no rerun needed)
├── Example_tutorial/               ← self-contained ATSAS + Python smoke test
│   ├── 2d.py                       ← needs numpy + matplotlib
│   ├── graph.py                    ← needs numpy + matplotlib
│   ├── H4WT_150Na.dat              ← experimental SAXS profile
│   ├── assignment.txt, protein.seq ← RANCH inputs
│   └── (20 example PDB structures)
├── SAXSData/
│   ├── H4WT_150Na.dat              ← wild-type H4 tail, 150 mM Na
│   └── H4KQ_150Na.dat              ← K-to-Q variant, 150 mM Na
├── getBestCurve.m                  ← MATLAB (needs Statistics toolbox fn)
├── make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m     ← MATLAB R2021+
├── plotEOMSAXScomparison.m         ← MATLAB R2021+
└── LICENSE.txt                     ← Apache 2.0
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L18), [README.md](README.md#L36), [README.md](README.md#L27-L28)

## Common Installation & Setup Issues

Beginners hit a small, well-defined set of failure modes with this stack. The table below maps each symptom to its verified cause and fix, drawing directly on the repository's own documentation and script comments:

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ranch` / `ffmaker` / `gajoe`: command not found | ATSAS binaries not on `PATH` | Add the ATSAS installation's binary directory to your shell `PATH` |
| MATLAB: `Undefined function 'tabulate'` | Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox not installed | Add the toolbox to your MATLAB installation; `tabulate` is called inside `getBestCurve.m` |
| `getBestCurve.m` cannot find `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files | GAJOE was run with workfile saving disabled | When GAJOE prompts "Save workfiles with the entire GA runs? (default: no)", answer **`y`** |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` expects a missing `best_curve` file | Running GAJOE v1.3-era assumptions against v2.x output | Use GAJOE v2.x consistently; the script calls `getBestCurve.m` to reconstruct the curve from GA cycle files |
| Python: `ModuleNotFoundError: numpy` / `matplotlib` | Packages not installed in the active interpreter | Run `python -m pip install numpy matplotlib` in the same environment you use to launch the scripts |
| MATLAB scripts point at wrong data | Path in "User-defined parameters" block not matched to your output | Edit the `dir` / `folder` variables at the top of each script — "mostly the paths just need to be matched" |

> [!TIP]
> The single most valuable habit from this table: when running GAJOE v2.x, always answer **`y`** to saving workfiles. `getBestCurve.m` — the foundation of the 2D histogram workflow — reconstructs the best curve from the per-cycle `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files that only exist if you saved them. Without that answer, the MATLAB pipeline cannot start.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L2-L9), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L6-L8), [README.md](README.md#L17), [README.md](README.md#L104-L106)

## Recommended Reading Path

You now have the full stack installed and verified. The logical progression through this documentation is: revisit [Overview](1-overview) and [Quick Start](2-quick-start) for high-level context if you haven't already, then proceed to the hands-on [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools), which walks through the RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE commands you just smoke-tested in detail. From there, [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview) explains how all the components you installed interact, and the Deep Dive pages (starting with [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation)) cover each ATSAS tool's behavior. If you took the optional AMBER path, continue to [MD Ensemble Generation with AMBER](18-md-ensemble-generation-with-amber); if you plan to extend beyond H4, [Extending Workflow to Other IDPs](19-extending-workflow-to-other-idps) is the natural endpoint.


# EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools



This page is a hands-on walkthrough of the **Ensemble Optimization Method (EOM)** pipeline using the ATSAS toolchain — `ranch` → `ffmaker` → `gajoe` — as implemented in the `Example_tutorial/` directory of this repository. The tutorial intentionally uses a minimal pool of **20 H4 histone tail conformations** so the entire pipeline can be executed end-to-end in minutes; the same four-step protocol scales directly to the production-size ensembles used in the full benchmark. Theory and per-tool internals are deliberately deferred to the Deep Dive pages linked at the end of each section.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [README.md](README.md#L3-L8)

## Prerequisites and Workspace Inventory

Before starting, install ATSAS (GAJOE v2.1 is recommended for CLI compatibility) and Python with `numpy` and `matplotlib`. Detailed installation guidance is covered in [Software Requirements and Installation](3-software-requirements-and-installation). All commands are executed from inside the `Example_tutorial/` directory.

The tutorial folder contains exactly six working files, each with a defined role in the pipeline:

| File | Role in the pipeline |
|---|---|
| `assignment.txt` | RANCH input: declares chain `A`, residues 1–26, as `disordered` |
| `protein.seq` | FASTA-format 26-residue H4 tail sequence consumed by RANCH |
| `H4WT_150Na.dat` | Experimental SAXS curve (53 q-points; columns Q, I(Q), Error) |
| `graph.py` | Plots experimental curve vs. GAJOE fit plus Rg / Dmax / Ree distributions |
| `2d.py` | Rg-vs-Ree scatter with marginal histograms, highlighting GAJOE-selected conformers |
| `pool_20/`, `GA001/` | Created at runtime by RANCH and GAJOE respectively |

The README also notes the directory ships with 20 example PDB structures as an alternative pool for FFMAKER, useful if you want to fit pre-generated models instead of RANCH output.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L36), [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2), [H4WT_150Na.dat](Example_tutorial/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L5), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L5), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L8-L9), [README.md](README.md#L60)

## Workflow at a Glance

The tutorial is a strict four-stage pipeline where each stage's output is the next stage's input. Understanding this data dependency chain before running anything prevents the most common setup mistakes:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Terminal in Example_tutorial/"] --> B["Step 1: RANCH<br/>20 randomized H4-tail conformations"]
    B --> C["pool_20/ CIF models"]
    C --> D["Step 2: FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles + size statistics"]
    D --> E["intensities_20.csv + size_statistics_20.csv"]
    E --> F["Step 3: GAJOE<br/>genetic-algorithm ensemble fit vs H4WT_150Na.dat"]
    F --> G["GA001/curve_1/<br/>fit profiles, distributions, selected pdbs/"]
    G --> H["Step 4: graph.py and 2d.py"]
    H --> I["saxs_fit.png, rg.png, dmax.png, ree.png, EOM_2D.png"]
```

Each numbered section below corresponds to one stage. All commands are quoted verbatim from the repository's tutorial so you can copy-paste them directly.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L118)

## Step 1 — RANCH: Generating the Conformational Pool

RANCH generates a randomized conformational pool from a sequence and an "assignment" descriptor. First create an output directory, then invoke `ranch` with the two bundled input files:

```bash
mkdir pool_20

ranch --repetitions 20 --prefix pool_20/model_ \
    --seed 12345 assignment.txt protein.seq
```

The two positional input files follow a minimal, verifiable format. `assignment.txt` contains the single line `A 1 26 disordered` — chain ID `A`, residue range 1 to 26, treated as a disordered region. `protein.seq` is a two-line FASTA record: header `>A` followed by the 26-residue sequence `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI` (the H4 tail construct analyzed in the case study).

| CLI flag | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `--repetitions` | `20` | Number of conformations generated |
| `--prefix` | `pool_20/model_` | Output directory and filename prefix |
| `--seed` | `12345` | PRNG seed → reproducible pool |
| positional 1 | `assignment.txt` | Chain/residue-range assignment |
| positional 2 | `protein.seq` | FASTA sequence |

**Output:** `pool_20/` containing 20 randomly generated conformations in CIF format. The fixed `--seed` makes the pool reproducible — remove it only if you want a new random draw.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L47), [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2)

For the theory behind random-pool construction, see [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation).

## Step 2 — FFMAKER: Theoretical SAXS Profiles and Size Statistics

FFMAKER converts every structure in the pool into two tabular artifacts consumed by GAJOE:

```bash
ffmaker --output intensities_20.csv \
    --pool size_statistics_20.csv pool_20/*.cif
```

| Output file | Contents |
|---|---|
| `intensities_20.csv` | Theoretical SAXS intensity profiles I(q) for all 20 conformations |
| `size_statistics_20.csv` | Per-conformation structural properties: Rg, Dmax, end-to-end distance (Ree), and volume |

Two practical notes verified in the repository: (1) to fit the bundled example PDB structures instead of the RANCH pool, simply replace the `pool_20/*.cif` glob with the path to those PDB files — the command structure is otherwise identical; (2) despite the `.csv` extension, downstream consumers in this repo parse these files with whitespace-token splitting that also tolerates commas, so either delimiter variant works.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L49-L60), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L14-L22), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L10-L11)

For how the profiles are computed, see [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles).

## Step 3 — GAJOE: Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Selection

GAJOE is the optimization core: it runs a genetic algorithm that selects the sub-ensemble of pool conformations whose averaged theoretical profile best matches the experimental curve `H4WT_150Na.dat`.

```bash
gajoe \
    --intensity intensities_20.csv \
    --size size_statistics_20.csv \
    --times 1 \
    --generation 100 \
    --ensemble 20 \
    --minimum 1 \
    --maximum 10 \
    --no-repeated \
    H4WT_150Na.dat
```

Every flag has a precise meaning — keep this table at hand when tuning runs:

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--intensity` | `intensities_20.csv` | FFMAKER theoretical profiles |
| `--size` | `size_statistics_20.csv` | Structural properties (Rg, Dmax, Ree, …) |
| `--times` | `1` | Number of independent GA runs |
| `--generation` | `100` | Generations per run |
| `--ensemble` | `20` | Candidate ensembles evaluated per generation |
| `--minimum` | `1` | Minimum conformations in a selected ensemble |
| `--maximum` | `10` | Maximum conformations in a selected ensemble |
| `--no-repeated` | — | Forbids duplicate conformations within an ensemble |
| positional | `H4WT_150Na.dat` | Experimental SAXS data being fitted |

**Output:** a result directory named `GA001` (then `GA002`, … for additional `--times` runs) containing:

| Artifact | Content |
|---|---|
| `profiles_*.fit` | Experimental data + fitted ensemble intensity, including χ² |
| `Rg_distr_*.txt` | Rg distributions of full pool and selected ensemble |
| `Size_distr_*.txt` | Corresponding Dmax distributions |
| `CaCa_distr_*.txt` | End-to-end distance distributions |
| `pdbs/` | Conformations selected by the GA |
| `logFile_*.log` | Optimization settings and results |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L62-L98)

The GA mechanics — selection, crossover, and ensemble fitness evaluation — are dissected in [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting), and every output file is cataloged in [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference).

## Step 4 — Visualizing Results with the Python Scripts

The final step renders GAJOE's numerical output into publication figures. Install the two dependencies, then run both scripts:

```bash
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib
python graph.py
python 2d.py
```

Both scripts read from fixed paths relative to `Example_tutorial/` and produce distinct figure families:

| Script | Inputs consumed | Figures produced |
|---|---|---|
| `graph.py` | `GA001/curve_1/profiles_*.fit` + `*_distr_*.dat` files | `saxs_fit.png`, `rg.png`, `dmax.png`, `ree.png` |
| `2d.py` | `size_statistics_20.csv` + `GA001/curve_1/pdbs/*.cif` | `EOM_2D.png` |

`graph.py` uses a purpose-built `read_numeric()` parser that silently skips non-numeric header lines and accepts both comma- and whitespace-delimited tokens — this is why GAJOE's raw `.fit` and distribution files, which begin with four text header lines, load without any preprocessing. The SAXS-fit branch plots experimental points with error bars against the fitted curve on a log intensity scale; the distribution branch plots every numeric column after the first (pool frequency and selected-ensemble frequency) for Rg, Dmax, and Ree.

`2d.py` takes a different route: it parses `size_statistics_20.csv` directly (columns 1, 3, and 6 hold Rg, Ree, and the structure name), then builds a boolean mask by matching the stems of CIF files in `GA001/curve_1/pdbs/` against pool names. The resulting figure is a GridSpec layout: a central Ree-vs-Rg scatter (full pool as filled coral points, EOM-selected structures as open dodgerblue circles) flanked by shared-axis marginal histograms, with 12 bins scaled to 1.1× the maximum of each quantity. A built-in assertion aborts execution if any selected structure cannot be found in the pool statistics file.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L118), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L7-L21), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L59), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L14-L41), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L43-L107)

> [!TIP]
> The `read_numeric()` helper truncates all rows to the minimum column count found (`np.array([row[:ncols] ...])`). If GAJOE ever emits trailing annotation columns in one row of a `.fit` file, the parser degrades gracefully rather than crashing — but verify column alignment if your fit curve looks shifted.

The plotting internals are documented in depth in [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots) and [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals).

## Cross-Checking Against the Bundled Reference Output

You do not need to guess what a successful run looks like: `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/` contains a full production-scale GAJOE result for the same H4 tail system. Its structure maps one-to-one onto the tutorial's expected output — `curve_1/` holds `profiles_001_1.fit`, the three distribution files plus `Volume_distr_001_1.txt`, `Size_list.txt`, `Ree_values.mat`, and per-cycle logs `GA_CYCLE_1.txt` through `GA_CYCLE_100.txt`.

Comparing the reference header against the tutorial's demo settings quantifies the scale gap you must close for quantitative work:

| Setting | Tutorial demo | Bundled reference run |
|---|---|---|
| Generations | 100 | 1000 |
| Ensembles per generation | 20 | 50 |
| Curves (independent GA runs) | 9 (reported in `.fit` header) | — |
| Pool size | 20 conformations | Full MD ensemble |
| χ² (best cycle) | — | 1.226 (cycle 29) |

The reference distribution files also reveal the four-line header + three-column layout (`value`, `Pool freq.`, `Sel. freq.`) that `graph.py` is designed to parse — and they show a real biological signature: the EOM-selected ensemble averages Rg ≈ 15.3 Å versus the pool's 13.8 Å, i.e., SAXS selection shifts the ensemble toward extended conformations.

Sources: [profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L6), [README.md](README.md#L12-L13), [README.md](README.md#L89)

## Troubleshooting

The tutorial's fixed-path assumptions are its main fragility. The table below maps observed symptoms to their verified root causes in the scripts:

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `rg.png` / `dmax.png` / `ree.png` silently missing after a successful run | `graph.py` globs `Rg_distr_*.dat` etc., but GAJOE output distribution files in this repo are named `*.txt` (and unmatched globs are skipped via `if not files: continue`) | Edit the three glob patterns in `graph.py` to `*.txt`, or rename outputs |
| `ValueError: No numeric data found in …` | Wrong `folder` path or empty glob match in `graph.py` | Point `folder` at the actual `GA001/curve_1/` produced by your run |
| `AssertionError: Some selected structures were not found in the pool!` | `size_statistics_20.csv` does not correspond to the pool GAJOE fitted (e.g., regenerated pool between steps) | Re-run FFMAKER on the exact pool passed to GAJOE |
| `FileNotFoundError` on `GA001/curve_1/pdbs` | `--times` / run-number mismatch — GAJOE creates `GA002`, `GA003`, … for later runs | Update paths in both scripts to the latest `GA00X/curve_N` |

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L40-L46), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L17-L18), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L40-L41), [README.md](README.md#L91-L98)

> [!TIP]
> Before automating multi-run pipelines, grep the distribution-file extension GAJOE v2.1 actually emits on your system (`ls GA001/curve_1/`). The README documents `*.txt` while `graph.py` defaults to `*.dat` globs — a one-character mismatch that produces silent, empty figure sets rather than errors.

## From Demonstration to Production

The 20-conformation pool exists solely to demonstrate mechanics. Both the README and the reference run's fit header encode the production recipe: increase generations and independent `--times` runs, and build the pool from a well-sampled MD trajectory (e.g., AMBER-generated ensembles as in the H4 benchmark) so that conformational space is adequately covered before GAJOE samples it. The MATLAB scripts in the repository root (`make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`, `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m`, `getBestCurve.m`) then extend this analysis to production-scale GAJOE folders.

**Recommended reading progression:**

1. Deepen each pipeline stage: [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation) → [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles) → [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) → [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference)
2. Master the analysis scripts: [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles), [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms), [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals)
3. Contextualize the science: [Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree](16-structural-descriptors-rg-dmax-ree) and [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study)
4. Reuse the workflow: [MD Ensemble Generation with AMBER](18-md-ensemble-generation-with-amber) and [Extending Workflow to Other IDPs](19-extending-workflow-to-other-idps)


# Architecture Overview



This page maps the structural organization of the **H4_tail_benchmarking** repository — a toolkit for benchmarking intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) structural ensembles from molecular dynamics (MD) against small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data, exemplified by the H4 histone tail. The architecture follows a deliberate separation: **data assets**, **ATSAS EOM pipeline artifacts**, and **analysis tooling** are organized into independent layers coupled only through well-defined file formats. Understanding this contract-driven design is essential before diving into individual pipeline stages or scripts. For a high-level introduction to the science, see [Overview](1-overview).

The repository is the companion to the paper: *Tong Wang, Egor S. Kolesnikov, Lois Pollack, Alexey V. Onufriev — "Combining atomistic simulation and solution scattering to reveal charge-driven histone H4 tail conformational changes"*.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L26)

## Repository Layout: A Three-Layer Architecture

The repository's directory tree encodes its conceptual architecture. Each top-level location serves exactly one architectural role, and the boundaries between them are strict:

| Layer | Location | Role | Key Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Experimental data** | `SAXSData/` | Raw SAXS profiles of wild-type and K-to-Q (charge-neutralized) H4 tail | `H4WT_150Na.dat`, `H4KQ_150Na.dat` |
| **RANCH inputs** | `Example_tutorial/` | Sequence definition files consumed by the conformational pool generator | `assignment.txt` (residue range assignment), `protein.seq` (26-residue H4 sequence) |
| **EOM output artifacts** | `ExampleData/.../GA001/` | Frozen GAJOE genetic algorithm results, ready for post-hoc analysis | 100 `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files, `profiles_001_1.fit`, size distributions, `Ree_values.mat` |
| **MATLAB analysis tooling** | repository root | Publication-quality ensemble analysis and SAXS comparison | `getBestCurve.m`, `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`, `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` |
| **Python plotting tooling** | `Example_tutorial/` | Lightweight visualization of the ATSAS tutorial workflow | `graph.py`, `2d.py` |

This layout encodes a key insight: the repository does **not** reimplement the EOM pipeline itself — that is delegated to the external ATSAS suite (RANCH, FFMAKER, GAJOE). Instead, the repository owns two things: (1) the *input contracts* that feed ATSAS, and (2) the *post-processing analysis* that extracts scientific conclusions from ATSAS output. The tutorial inputs illustrate this minimalism — the entire RANCH configuration is a single line declaring residue A, positions 1–26, as `disordered`:

```
A 1 26 disordered
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L27-L40), [assignment.txt](/Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [protein.seq](/Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2), [getBestCurve.m](/getBestCurve.m#L6-L9)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The complete system spans two worlds: the **external ATSAS pipeline** (steps 1–3, installed separately) and the **in-repo analysis layer** (step 4). The Mermaid diagram below shows the flow of artifacts between them, with in-repo components highlighted:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ATSAS["ATSAS Suite (external)"]
        RANCH["RANCH<br/>pool generation"] -->|pool/*.cif| FF["FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles"]
        FF -->|intensities + size_statistics| GA["GAJOE<br/>genetic algorithm fitting"]
    end

    EXP[("Experimental SAXS<br/>.dat files")] --> GA
    MD[("MD ensemble<br/>PDB structures")] --> RANCH

    subgraph REPO["This repository"]
        GA -->|"GA_CYCLE_*.txt<br/>(100 GA runs)"| GBC["getBestCurve.m<br/>best-curve reconstruction"]
        GBC -->|"[PDB#, frequency]"| M2D["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>2D histograms + JSD"]
        GA -->|"profiles_*.fit"| PEQ["plotEOMSAXScomparison.m<br/>SAXS fit + Kratky + residuals"]
        GA -->|"*.fit, *_distr_*.dat"| GPY["graph.py<br/>SAXS curve + distributions"]
        FF -->|"size_statistics csv"| D2["2d.py<br/>Rg–Ree scatter + marginals"]
        GA -->|"pdbs/ selection"| D2
    end

    M2D --> OUT1[("Ensemble comparison plots<br/>+ Jensen-Shannon divergence")]
    PEQ --> OUT2[("Fit quality diagnostics")]
```

Three data contracts cross the ATSAS/repository boundary. First, GAJOE's `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` logs record every generation's best ensembles as chi² values paired with structure index chains (e.g., `-122-180-257-374-...`), spanning ~20,000 lines per run — this is the raw material `getBestCurve.m` mines. Second, `profiles_*.fit` carries the experimental data and the CRYSOL-computed ensemble fit in one file, which both MATLAB and Python plotting consume. Third, FFMAKER's size statistics table (Rg, Dmax, Ree, volume per conformation) provides the structural descriptors that populate all histograms and scatter plots.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L30-L40), [GA_CYCLE_1.txt](/ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_1.txt#L1-L15)

## The Analysis Tooling Layer: MATLAB vs. Python

The repository ships **two independent tooling implementations** over the same GAJOE output format, targeting different depths of analysis:

| Dimension | MATLAB scripts (root) | Python scripts (`Example_tutorial/`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Entry points** | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`, `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | `graph.py`, `2d.py` |
| **Shared helper** | `getBestCurve.m` (function) | Inline parsing (`read_numeric`) |
| **Primary inputs** | `GA_CYCLE_*.txt`, `Size_list.txt`, `Ree_values.mat`, `profiles_001_1.fit` | `profiles_*.fit`, `*_distr_*.dat`, `size_statistics_20.csv`, `pdbs/*.cif` |
| **Outputs** | Rg–Ree and Dmax–Rg joint distributions with marginals; SAXS fit, Kratky plot, residuals; JSD scalars | `saxs_fit.png`, `rg.png`, `dmax.png`, `ree.png`; Rg–Ree scatter with marginals |
| **Quantitative analysis** | Yes — Jensen-Shannon divergence between MD pool and EOM pool | No — visualization only |
| **Dependencies** | MATLAB R2021+, Statistics functions | `numpy`, `matplotlib` |
| **Intended use** | Publication analysis of full-scale MD ensembles | Quick verification of the 20-conformation tutorial run |

The division of labor is intentional rather than redundant. The MATLAB suite is the scientific workhorse: it handles the benchmarking-scale GAJOE output (100 GA runs × 100 generations) and computes the Jensen-Shannon divergence that quantifies how much SAXS refinement shifts ensemble distributions. The Python pair covers the ATSAS-native tutorial workflow, using robust heuristic parsing (skipping non-numeric header lines, tolerating comma or space delimiters) that works directly against fresh GAJOE output directories.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L30-L40), [graph.py](/Example_tutorial/graph.py#L1-L21), [2d.py](/Example_tutorial/2d.py#L1-L41)

## Component Anatomy: The Best-Curve Reconstruction Bridge

One component deserves architectural attention because it solves a **version-compatibility problem** in the toolchain. `getBestCurve.m` exists because GAJOE v2.1 — unlike v1.3 — no longer emits a `best_curve.txt` summary of which conformations the genetic algorithm selected. This function recreates that lost artifact from the workfile logs, requiring the GAJOE option *"Save workfiles with the entire GA runs"* to be enabled during fitting.

Its algorithm is a two-phase aggregation:

1. **Extraction** — for each of the `nRuns` GA cycles, read `GA_CYCLE_<i>.txt` with a `'-'` delimiter, take the last `curvesPerEnsemble` rows (the final generation's population), flatten into a single list of selected structure indices, and drop `NaN` padding from variable-length ensembles.
2. **Aggregation** — tabulate selection frequencies across all runs via `categorical`/`tabulate`, returning an `[PDB_number, frequency]` matrix that downstream scripts treat exactly like the historical `best_curve.txt`.

> [!TIP]
> The frequency column is load-bearing: `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` expands each selected structure by its selection count using `repmat` before building the EOM ensemble histograms. If you re-run GAJOE with different run counts, you must update **both** `nRuns` and `curvesPerEnsemble` in the caller's parameter block — the parser slices the last N rows by position, so mismatched values silently corrupt the ensemble reconstruction.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](/getBestCurve.m#L1-L42), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](/make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L55)

## Internal Script Architecture: Parameter Block Pattern

Both MATLAB entry scripts follow an identical internal structure that you should recognize before modifying them. Each script is organized into `%%`-delimited cell blocks with a strict execution order:

| Block | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` |
|---|---|---|
| **1. User-defined parameters** | `dir`, `nRuns`, `curvesPerEnsemble`, axis limits, histogram bins, font sizes | `folder`, plot colour (WT orange vs. KQ blue), axis limits |
| **2. Data ingestion** | `getBestCurve()` call + `Size_list.txt` (cols: Rg, Dmax) + `Ree_values.mat` | `readmatrix` on `SAXSData/*.dat` (4 header lines) and `profiles_*.fit` (1 header line, col 4 = ensemble fit) |
| **3. Ensemble expansion** | `repmat` frequency-weighted expansion of selected structures | — |
| **4. Visualization** | Two joint-distribution figures (Ree–Rg, Dmax–Rg), each with normalized marginal histograms; printed mean ± SEM statistics | SAXS fit overlay, Kratky transform (q²I(q)), residuals via `interp1` alignment of experimental points onto the fit grid |
| **5. Quantification** | Jensen-Shannon divergence for Rg and Ree distributions, with Shannon entropy `H(p)` subfunction | — |

All configuration lives in Block 1 — per the README, "mostly the paths just need to be matched." No script accepts command-line arguments; every run is an edit-and-execute interaction. The JSD block is self-contained: it histogram-normalizes both distributions to PDFs on shared bin edges and applies the divergence formula `JSD = H(0.5·p₁ + 0.5·p₂) − 0.5·H(p₁) − 0.5·H(p₂)`, with `0·log(0)` handled by zeroing NaN entropy contributions.

> [!TIP]
> The two scripts deliberately share no code beyond `getBestCurve.m` — a conscious trade-off favoring standalone readability over DRY. When adapting the workflow to a new IDP, you will typically duplicate a script and change one parameter block rather than refactor shared logic, so keep parameter blocks at the top exactly where they are.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](/make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L130), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](/make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L234), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](/plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L80), [README.md](/README.md#L40-L42)

## File Format Contracts

The entire architecture hinges on ATSAS-standard file formats. These are the interfaces every script depends on — knowing them lets you trace any data flow in the system:

| File | Producer | Consumer | Content Contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GA_CYCLE_<i>.txt` | GAJOE v2.1 (workfiles) | `getBestCurve.m` | Generations of best ensembles: rank, chi², structure-index chain; final-generation rows are the selected ensemble |
| `Size_list.txt` | GAJOE | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | Per-conformation structural table; column 2 = Rg, column 3 = Dmax |
| `Ree_values.mat` | Companion preprocessing (`pdb_Rmeas.m`) | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | End-to-end distance vector `R` indexed by conformation number |
| `profiles_001_1.fit` | GAJOE/CRYSOL | `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m`, `graph.py` | Columns: q, experimental I(q), error, ensemble-fitted I(q) |
| `Rg_distr_*.txt`, `Size_distr_*.txt`, `CaCa_distr_*.txt` | GAJOE | `graph.py` | Pool vs. selected-ensemble distribution curves per descriptor |
| `size_statistics_20.csv` | FFMAKER | `2d.py` | Space-delimited: Rg, ReE, ..., conformation filename (col 6) |
| `assignment.txt` + `protein.seq` | User | RANCH | Sequence range/type assignment and FASTA-style sequence |

Note the one asymmetry: `Ree_values.mat` is not produced by ATSAS at all — it comes from a separate measurement of end-to-end distances over the full MD pool's PDBs, which is why the pool carries three descriptor sources (two from ATSAS, one computed locally).

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](/make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L39), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](/plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16), [graph.py](/Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L49), [2d.py](/Example_tutorial/2d.py#L8-L30)

## Architectural Principles Summary

Three design decisions govern everything in this repository. **Delegation over reimplementation**: the EOM pipeline itself (RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE) is owned by ATSAS; this repo provides inputs and interprets outputs, keeping it usable with ATSAS v2.1+ without duplicating physics. **File-format coupling**: components never call each other directly — they exchange data exclusively through ATSAS-standard files, so any script can be run independently and against any conforming GAJOE output directory. **Explicit-configuration scripts**: all tunables sit in visible parameter blocks rather than hidden defaults or CLI flags, making the publication-reproducible settings auditable at a glance.

The consequence is a system with near-zero coupling surface: you can swap in your own GAJOE run (e.g., H4KQ instead of H4WT) by changing one path string, or adopt the Python tools for a different ATSAS project entirely.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L30-L42), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](/make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L11-L31)

## Where to Go Next

With the architectural map in hand, follow these entry points by goal:

- **Understand the pipeline stages** that produce the artifacts analyzed here: start with [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation), then [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles) and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).
- **Work with the MATLAB tooling**: the best-curve bridge is dissected in [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles), the joint-distribution plots in [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms), and the divergence metric in [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification).
- **Run the pipeline yourself**: follow [Quick Start](2-quick-start) and the step-by-step [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools), which exercises the Python path (`graph.py`, `2d.py`).
- **Apply the framework to your own protein**: see [Extending Workflow to Other IDPs](19-extending-workflow-to-other-idps), grounded in the concrete [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).

# RANCH Conformational Pool Generation



RANCH is the first executable stage of the Ensemble Optimization Method (EOM) workflow in this repository: it converts a bare protein sequence definition into a pool of randomly generated 3D conformations. This page documents RANCH's role in the pipeline, its exact input contract as used in the H4 histone tail tutorial, its command-line parameters, the artifacts it produces, and the pool-design trade-offs between reproducibility and statistical power. RANCH itself is part of the external ATSAS suite — this repository consumes it, and the tutorial in the README demonstrates it end-to-end with a deliberately small 20-conformation pool.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L36), [README.md](README.md#L23-L25)

## Role in the EOM Pipeline

The EOM pipeline in this repository is a strict three-stage sequence: **RANCH** (generate), **FFMAKER** (compute theoretical SAXS profiles), and **GAJOE** (genetic-algorithm ensemble fitting against experimental data). RANCH is the only stage that creates structural data from scratch — everything downstream operates on the pool it emits. The two files RANCH requires (`assignment.txt` and `protein.seq`) are pure text inputs checked into `Example_tutorial/`, and its output (`pool_20/` of CIF files) is consumed positionally by FFMAKER via a glob.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L34-L36), [README.md](README.md#L38-L54)

The diagram below shows the data flow. RANCH takes the two text inputs, emits numbered CIF conformations into `pool_20/`, and those files become FFMAKER's input glob (`pool_20/*.cif`). FFMAKER then produces the intensity and size-statistics CSVs that GAJOE fits against the experimental curve `H4WT_150Na.dat`. Steps 2 and 3 are covered in detail on [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles) and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph IN["RANCH inputs (text)"]
        SEQ["protein.seq<br/>chain sequence"]
        ASG["assignment.txt<br/>chain / residue layout"]
    end
    subgraph S1["Step 1 — RANCH"]
        GEN["random pool generator"]
    end
    subgraph POOL["pool_20/"]
        CIF["model_1.cif ... model_20.cif"]
    end
    FF["Step 2 — FFMAKER:<br/>intensities_20.csv<br/>size_statistics_20.csv"]
    GA["Step 3 — GAJOE:<br/>GA001/"]
    EXP["H4WT_150Na.dat<br/>(experimental SAXS)"]

    SEQ --> GEN
    ASG --> GEN
    GEN --> CIF
    CIF --> FF
    FF --> GA
    EXP --> GA
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L47), [README.md](README.md#L51-L58)

Note that RANCH is not the only way to obtain a conformational pool. The repository's broader benchmarking workflow also compares pools derived from all-atom molecular dynamics; that alternative source is documented in [MD Ensemble Generation with AMBER](18-md-ensemble-generation-with-amber). Within the EOM tutorial itself, however, RANCH defines the starting ensemble.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L7), [README.md](README.md#L15-L16)

## The Input Contract: `assignment.txt` and `protein.seq`

RANCH requires exactly two positional input files, both present in `Example_tutorial/`. The README explicitly identifies them as "two input files (`assignment.txt`, `protein.seq`) required by RANCH". They are deliberately minimal — together they contain no 3D data at all, only the sequence identity and a declaration of how each chain should be modeled.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L34-L36), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3)

| File | Role | Format | Tutorial content |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protein.seq` | Defines the amino acid sequence per chain | FASTA-style: `>A` header line, then one-letter residue codes | 26 residues: `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI` (H4 histone tail) |
| `assignment.txt` | Declares each chain's residue span and structural type | One whitespace-delimited line per chain: `chain start end type` | Single line: `A 1 26 disordered` |

Sources: [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [README.md](README.md#L7-L8)

The assignment file for the H4 tail is a single line — `A 1 26 disordered` — which decomposes as follows:

| Column | Value in tutorial | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `A` | Chain identifier, matching the `>A` header in `protein.seq` |
| 2 | `1` | First residue of the modeled segment |
| 3 | `26` | Last residue of the modeled segment |
| 4 | `disordered` | The segment is treated as a flexible/disordered region, not a rigid body |

Sources: [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1), [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2)

The two files are linked by the chain identifier, and the residue span must be consistent with the sequence it indexes. In the tutorial both constraints hold exactly: the `>A` header matches chain `A`, and the declared span `1–26` equals the actual 26-residue sequence length.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ASG["assignment.txt (one line per chain)"]
        A1["col 1: A — chain ID"]
        A2["col 2: 1 — first residue"]
        A3["col 3: 26 — last residue"]
        A4["col 4: disordered — segment type"]
    end
    subgraph SEQ["protein.seq (FASTA-style)"]
        S1[">A — chain header"]
        S2["SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI<br/>26 residues"]
    end
    A1 -. must match .- S1
    A2 -. span covers .- S2
    A3 -. 26 = sequence length .- S2
```

> [!TIP]
