The MATLAB route assumes the EOM pipeline (RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE, documented in [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools) and the deep-dive pages on [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation), [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles), and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting)) has completed. From there:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Run GAJOE v2.1 on the pool"] --> B["Answer y to:<br/>'Save workfiles with the entire GA runs?'"]
    B --> C["Compute Ree for every pool structure<br/>run pdb_Rmeas.m on the full-pool PDBs<br/>→ writes Ree_values.mat into the GAJOE dir"]
    C --> D["Edit 'User-defined parameters' block:<br/>dir, nRuns, curvesPerEnsemble,<br/>axis limits, bin counts, fonts"]
    D --> E["Run make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m"]
    E --> F["Read two figures,<br/>console mean ± SEM,<br/>JSD_rg and JSD_r"]
```

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Error opening `GA_CYCLE_1.txt` | Workfiles were not saved during GAJOE | Re-run GAJOE answering `y` to the save-workfiles prompt |
| Error on `load(Ree_values.mat)` | `pdb_Rmeas.m` was not run over the full pool | Generate `Ree_values.mat` first (per the script header comment) |
| Empty/scattered EOM overlay | `nRuns` / `curvesPerEnsemble` mismatch with the actual GAJOE run | Match values to what was entered at the GAJOE prompts |
| Points clipped from the panel | Data outside `xlim_Dmax` / `ylim_Rg` / `xlim_R` | Widen axis limits for the new system's descriptor ranges |
| Histograms barely overlap in scale | Pool (22) vs ensemble (15) bin counts and peak normalization | Treat marginals as shape guides; rely on JSD for quantitative comparison |

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L2-L8), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L31), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L7-L9), [README.md](README.md#L23-L25)

## Interpreting the Output

Read the figures as a **selection-bias map**. Blue circles clustering toward one corner of the joint panel (e.g., low Rg with short Ree) means the SAXS curve preferentially selects compact members; spread across the orange cloud indicates the data cannot discriminate among pool conformers. The marginals make this univariate: a narrowed blue Rg peak versus the broad orange pool peak signals that SAXS constrains size but perhaps not shape, while concurrent narrowing in Ree and Rg marginals suggests coupled compaction. The printed SEMs tell you whether the blue mean shift is resolvable, and JSD condenses the whole comparison into one number per descriptor — compare `JSD_rg` against `JSD_r` to ask whether size or extension dominates the SAXS selection signal.

For the H4 histone tail context in which this example data was produced — and how WT vs K-to-Q charge-neutralized variants are compared with these tools — see [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study). Descriptor definitions and their physical meaning for IDPs are covered in [Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree](16-structural-descriptors-rg-dmax-ree).

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L58-L130), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L234)

- **Downstream**: [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification) expands on the entropy-based metric computed at the end of this script; [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals) covers the companion script `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` for the curve-level view.

# Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification



This page documents the **Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD)** analytics stage embedded in `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`, which quantifies — as a single scalar per structural descriptor — how far the SAXS-refined ensemble selected by GAJOE diverges from the full MD conformational pool. The divergence is computed independently for the **radius of gyration (Rg)** and **end-to-end distance (Ree)** distributions and printed to the MATLAB command window as `JSD_rg` and `JSD_r`. The stage was appended to the script in September 2025, with the method attributed to `plotIterativeAnalysis.m` from RNA-condensates analysis software. This page covers only the divergence mathematics, its implementation, and its numerical behavior; the visual 2D histograms produced by the same script are covered in [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms).

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L187), [README.md](README.md#L13-L14)

## Pipeline Position and Concept Map

The JSD computation is the **terminal stage** of `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`: it runs after both publication figures have been rendered, reusing the same ensemble vectors (`pool.*` and `gajoe.*`) that drive the plots. Conceptually, the stage chains three transformations — ensemble construction from GA output, probability discretization via histogram binning, and a three-term entropy decomposition — producing two scalars. Note that the repository's Python utilities (`graph.py`, `2d.py`) are purely graphical and compute no divergence; MATLAB is the quantitative home of JSD in this codebase.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Size_list.txt<br/>(per-PDB Rg, Dmax)"] --> C["pool.rg, pool.dmax<br/>(full MD pool)"]
    B["Ree_values.mat<br/>(per-PDB Ree)"] --> D["pool.r<br/>(full MD pool)"]
    E["GA_CYCLE_1..100.txt"] --> F["getBestCurve.m<br/>PDB × frequency table"]
    F --> G["repmat expansion<br/>by selection frequency"]
    G --> I["gajoe.rg, gajoe.r<br/>(SAXS-refined EOM pool)"]
    C --> H["histcounts(...,'pdf')<br/>p1 (MD) / p2 (EOM)"]
    I --> H
    D --> H
    H --> J["JSD = H(½p₁+½p₂) − ½H(p₁) − ½H(p₂)"]
    J --> K["JSD_rg — Rg distributions"]
    J --> L["JSD_r — Ree distributions"]
```

The `pool.*` vectors describe the entire conformational pool generated by MD, while the `gajoe.*` vectors reconstruct the *weighted* ensemble selected by the genetic algorithm — each selected structure is repeated as many times as it appears across the 100 GA runs. This weighting is what makes the divergence meaningful: it compares the **unbiased MD distribution** against the **SAXS-weighted selection**, revealing which conformational sub-populations SAXS data pulled toward.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L189), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L29-L37), [Example_tutorial/2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L1-L20)

## Mathematical Formulation

For two discretized distributions P (MD pool) and Q (EOM pool), the script computes the Jensen-Shannon divergence via the **mixture-entropy decomposition**:

$$\mathrm{JSD}(P \,\|\, Q) = H\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}P + \tfrac{1}{2}Q\right) - \tfrac{1}{2}H(P) - \tfrac{1}{2}H(Q)$$

The code maps each term directly to named variables: `JSD1 = H(0.5.*p1 + 0.5.*p2)` is the mixture entropy, `JSD2 = 0.5.*H(p1)` and `JSD3 = 0.5.*H(p2)` are the halved component entropies, and the final value is `JSD1 - JSD2 - JSD3`. Shannon entropy itself is delegated to a local subfunction `H(p)` that returns `-sum(p.*log(p))`, with the standard convention **0·log(0) = 0** enforced by replacing `NaN` entries (MATLAB evaluates `0*log(0)` to `NaN` since `log(0) = -Inf`) before summation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["P — MD pool<br/>H(P) → JSD2"] --> S["JSD = JSD1 − JSD2 − JSD3"]
    Q["Q — EOM pool<br/>H(Q) → JSD3"] --> S
    M["Mixture M = ½P+½Q<br/>H(M) → JSD1"] --> S
```

Because the entropy uses MATLAB's natural `log`, divergence values are expressed in **nats**, bounded by **[0, ln 2] ≈ [0, 0.6931]**. JSD equals 0 if and only if the two discretized distributions are identical, is symmetric in P and Q, and its square root is a true metric — properties that distinguish it from the asymmetric, unbounded KL divergence.

| Property | Value / Behavior | Basis in Code |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | H(M) − ½H(P) − ½H(Q) | `JSD1 - JSD2 - JSD3` |
| Logarithm base | e (nats) | `log` in subfunction `H` |
| Range | [0, ln 2] ≈ [0, 0.693] | natural-log bound |
| Symmetry | Symmetric in P, Q | mixture is `0.5.*p1 + 0.5.*p2` |
| Empty-bin handling | contributes 0 to entropy | `body(isnan(body)) = 0` |
| Descriptors covered | Rg and Ree only | Dmax vectors exist but no JSD block |

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L202-L206), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L221-L225), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L229-L234)

## Implementation Walkthrough

The stage occupies lines 185–234 and is deliberately minimal: two nearly identical blocks (one per descriptor) plus one shared subfunction. A key operational detail is the opening statement `figure('Visible','off')` — the `histogram()` calls render figures as a side effect, so the author suppresses their visibility to keep the divergence computation non-intrusive after the publication figures have already been produced. Both result variables are assigned **without a trailing semicolon** (`JSD_rg = ...`, `JSD_r = ...`), so values echo to the command window; nothing is persisted to disk automatically.

| Step | Lines | MATLAB Operation | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suppress plotting | 189 | `figure('Visible','off')` | hide histogram side-effects |
| Discretize MD Rg | 191–192 | `histcounts(pool.rg, binsRg, 'Normalization','pdf')` | density vector p1 |
| Discretize EOM Rg | 195–196 | `histcounts(gajoe.rg, binsRg, 'Normalization','pdf')` | density vector p2 |
| Rg divergence | 202–206 | entropy decomposition | prints `JSD_rg` |
| Discretize + Ree divergence | 210–225 | same recipe with `binsR` | prints `JSD_r` |
| Entropy subfunction | 229–234 | `H = -sum(p.*log(p))` with NaN→0 | Shannon entropy, 0·log(0)=0 |

Two commented-out lines (`%mdpool = mdpool ./ max(mdpool)` and its EOM counterpart) record that **peak-normalization** was considered and abandoned in favor of `'Normalization','pdf'` — i.e., the histogram is scaled to integrate to unity rather than to peak at 1. This matters for reproducibility: switching normalization changes the absolute scale of reported values, so results from different script versions are not directly comparable.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L189-L206), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L209-L225), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L193-L197)

## Inputs and Data Provenance

The divergence stage consumes four ensemble vectors assembled earlier in the same script. The full-pool descriptors come directly from GAJOE/FFMAKER output files in the results directory, while the EOM-side descriptors are *reconstructed* by expanding a PDB-number × frequency table across all 100 GA cycles — essentially resurrecting the `best_curve.txt` file that GAJOE v2 no longer emits. This reconstruction requires that GAJOE was run with **"Save workfiles with the entire GA runs" set to yes**, since the per-cycle selection files are the raw material.

| Variable | Source File | Construction |
|---|---|---|
| `pool.rg`, `pool.dmax` | `Size_list.txt` (cols 2, 3) | direct `importdata` column slice |
| `pool.r` | `Ree_values.mat` (variable `R`) | loaded from workspace file |
| `gajoe.rg`, `gajoe.r` | `GA_CYCLE_1..100.txt` via `getBestCurve` | `repmat` each PDB's descriptor by its GA selection frequency |

`getBestCurve` parses each cycle file with a `'-'` delimiter, keeps the last `curvesPerEnsemble` rows (the selected structures), flattens all 100 cycles into one list, and tabulates occurrence frequencies into the two-column `[PDBnum, frequency]` matrix. Because frequencies accumulate over `nRuns = 100` independent GA runs, the EOM distribution is effectively a **consensus ensemble** — a structure selected in many cycles contributes many copies, sharpening the corresponding histogram peaks and lowering entropy relative to a single-run selection.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L25), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L31-L37), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L42-L55), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L21-L29), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L31-L41)

For the full mechanics of that reconstruction, see [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles); for how GA cycles are produced, see [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).

## Bin Configuration and Numerical Behavior

Bin settings are the dominant tunable of this stage, and the script uses **different bin counts for plotting versus divergence**. The rendered marginal histograms use `binsRg`/`binsDmax`/`binsR` = 22 for the full pool but `gajoeHistBins` = 15 for the EOM ensemble; the JSD stage, however, recomputes both distributions from raw vectors with the *same* count (`binsRg` = 22 for Rg, `binsR` = 22 for Ree) — it does not reuse the plotted histograms. Any change to these user parameters at the top of the script silently alters reported divergence values.

| Context | MD Pool Bins | EOM Pool Bins | Normalization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plotted marginals (first figure) | 22 (`binsR`) | 15 (`gajoeHistBins`) | peak-normalized (BinCounts/max) |
| Plotted marginals (second figure) | 22 (`binsRg`/`binsDmax`) | 15 (`gajoeHistBins`) | raw counts |
| **JSD computation (Rg)** | **22 (`binsRg`)** | **22 (`binsRg`)** | `'pdf'` (integrates to 1) |
| **JSD computation (Ree)** | **22 (`binsR`)** | **22 (`binsR`)** | `'pdf'` (integrates to 1) |

> [!TIP]
> `histcounts(x, nbins)` derives bin edges from each array's **own min–max range**, so `p1` and `p2` are evaluated on different grids: the element-wise mixture `0.5.*p1 + 0.5.*p2` implicitly assumes bin alignment that is not guaranteed. For rigorous cross-ensemble comparisons, compute shared edges first (e.g., `edges = linspace(min([pool.rg; gajoe.rg]), max([pool.rg; gajoe.rg]), binsRg+1))` and call `histcounts(x, edges, 'Normalization','pdf')` for both vectors.

> [!TIP]
> The `'pdf'` normalization makes bin heights integrate to 1 (Σp·Δ = 1), but the entropy sum uses the heights directly as probability masses. Reported JSD values are therefore best treated as **relative comparators under a fixed binning recipe** — consistent across runs of this script — rather than absolute entropies; magnitude depends on the chosen bin count and descriptor ranges.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L12-L25), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L190-L197)

## Interpreting JSD_rg and JSD_r

The two printed scalars answer complementary questions about the SAXS-driven selection. `JSD_rg` measures how much compactness (Rg) was redistributed by fitting to SAXS data, while `JSD_r` measures redistribution of chain extension (Ree); for the H4 histone-tail case study, shifts in these descriptors encode the charge-driven conformational changes the pipeline was built to detect. The script additionally prints mean ± standard error for both descriptors of both ensembles immediately after the first figure, giving the directional context (which ensemble is more compact/extended) that a raw JSD lacks.

| Observation | Likely Interpretation | Suggested Action |
|---|---|---|
| JSD ≈ 0 | EOM ensemble statistically indistinguishable from MD pool | selection not driven by this descriptor; check the other one |
| 0 < JSD ≪ ln 2 | partial sub-population shift | compare printed means to identify direction |
| JSD approaching ln 2 (0.693) | distribution supports nearly disjoint | inspect axes limits and bin overlap; verify pool completeness |
| Value shifts when bins changed | resolution-dependent estimate | fix one binning recipe for all reported comparisons |

Because results are command-window output only, a reproducible workflow should capture them manually or add a semicolon plus explicit logging (e.g., writing `[JSD_rg JSD_r]` to a results file) before scaling the analysis across multiple GA result folders such as `GA001`, `GA002`, …

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L109-L128), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L202-L206), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L221-L225)

## Where to Go Next

Within the MATLAB analysis track, the natural continuation is the SAXS-facing half of the validation: [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals) visualizes *how well* the selected ensemble fits the experimental profile whose selection pressure produced the divergence you just quantified. For the structural-theory background behind the Rg/Ree descriptors being compared, see [Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree](16-structural-descriptors-rg-dmax-ree); for the upstream GA machinery that defines the EOM ensemble, see [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) and its companion [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference).


# SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals



This page documents `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m`, the terminal visualization stage of the MATLAB analysis chain. The script produces a three-panel figure suite that answers a single question from three angles: **how well does the GAJOE-optimized ensemble reproduce the experimental SAXS curve of the H4 histone tail?** Panel 1 overlays the fitted ensemble intensity on the raw experiment, Panel 2 recasts both into Kratky form to expose conformational character (compact vs. disordered), and Panel 3 plots point-wise residuals against the experimental error band. It is a self-contained plotting script — no fitting, no computation of ensemble statistics — intended to be run after GAJOE fitting is complete.

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L1-L16), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L25-L97)

## Position in the Analysis Pipeline

The script sits at the end of the EOM pipeline and depends on exactly two artifacts: the `.fit` file written by GAJOE during the genetic-algorithm fit (containing the best cycle's reconstructed ensemble profile), and the original experimental scattering data in `SAXSData/`. Everything the script draws is derived from these two files — it performs no IO beyond `readmatrix` and no numerical fitting of its own. The `.fit` file consumed here is the same artifact catalogued in the [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference), and its content traces back through the fitting described in [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["FFMAKER theoretical curves (.int)"] --> B["GAJOE genetic algorithm fit"]
    B --> C["profiles_001_1.fit (cycle 29, Chi² 1.226)"]
    D["Experimental H4WT_150Na.dat"] --> E
    C --> E["plotEOMSAXScomparison.m"]
    E --> F["Panel 1: I(q) fit overlay"]
    E --> G["Panel 2: Kratky q²I(q)"]
    E --> H["Panel 3: residuals + error band"]
```

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L9-L16), [profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L5)

## Input Contract: Two Files, Four Columns Each

The script's entire data model rests on two `readmatrix` calls with strict header-skipping rules. The experimental file `H4WT_150Na.dat` uses 4 header lines (a `### DATA` banner, blank comment lines, and the `Q, I(Q), Error` column legend), after which follow 53 whitespace-separated data rows. The GAJOE output `profiles_001_1.fit` uses exactly 1 header line — a summary line reporting `CYCLE: 29`, `Chi^2: 1.226`, `GENER.: 1000`, `ENSEMBLES: 50`, `CURVES: 9` — followed by 4 numeric columns: q, experimental intensity, experimental error, and fitted ensemble intensity.

| File | Path | Header lines | Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 | Column 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Experimental | `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat` | 4 | q (Å⁻¹) | I(q) | σ(q) | — |
| GAJOE fit | `ExampleData/.../GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit` | 1 | q (Å⁻¹) | I_exp(q) | error (≈1e-17) | I_fit(q) |

The critical mapping happens on line 28: `crysolEOM = [fitFile(:,1), fitFile(:,4)]` — the script binds **column 4** (the fitted ensemble profile), *not* column 2 (which merely echoes the experimental intensity into the `.fit` file for convenience). Everything downstream is drawn from this two-column `crysolEOM` matrix.

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L27-L28), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L5), [profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1-L2)

> [!TIP]
> The `.fit` file's third column (experimental error) contains near-zero values on the order of 1e-17 — visible in the raw file as `1.552584e-017`, `3.479447e-018`, etc. This is why the script **ignores that column entirely** and, for the residual panel's error band, re-derives σ(q) from the original `SAXSData/*.dat` file via interpolation. If you adapt this script to new data, never feed `fitFile(:,3)` into the error band: GAJOE's error column in `.fit` output is not the experimental uncertainty you want to plot.

## The Three Diagnostic Panels

The script generates one standalone figure and one stacked two-subplot figure. Each panel applies a different mathematical transform to the *same* two-column data, and each answers a distinct diagnostic question:

| Panel | Transform applied | Figure layout | Question answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fit overlay | none — raw I(q) vs q | Standalone `figure` | Does the ensemble curve track the experiment over the measured q-range? |
| Kratky plot | I(q) → q²·I(q) | `subplot(2,1,1)` | Does the ensemble show globular (bell-shaped) or disordered (rising/plateau) behavior? |
| Residuals | I_exp − I_fit at matched q | `subplot(2,1,2)` | Are deviations structured (systematic) or confined to the noise level? |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DATA["crysolEOM = [q, I_fit] + expData = [q, I, σ]"] --> P1
    DATA --> P2
    DATA --> P3
    P1["Panel 1 — direct overlay<br/>errorbar(I, σ) vs plot(I_fit)"] --> Q1{"Q: overall agreement"}
    P2["Panel 2 — Kratky transform<br/>multiply both series by q²"] --> Q2{"Q: compact vs disordered"}
    P3["Panel 3 — difference<br/>interp1(I_exp onto q_fit) − I_fit"] --> Q3{"Q: systematic error?"}
```

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L25-L28), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L47-L48), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L66-L67)

### Panel 1 — SAXS Fit Overlay

The first figure plots the experimental data as gray symmetric error bars (`errorbar(expData(:,1), expData(:,2), expData(:,3))`, where column 3 of the `.dat` file supplies σ) with the GAJOE ensemble profile as a thick line in a user-selected accent color (orange `[238 68 0]/255` for H4WT; a commented-out navy alternative exists for H4KQ). Both series share the same q-axis, clipped to `xlim_SAXS = [0 0.3]`. The legend distinguishes `SAXS experiment` from `EOM ensemble`, and axis labels use MATLAB's LaTeX interpreter for proper Å⁻¹ typesetting.

One caveat is stated in the script's own header comment: the scale factors between experiment and fit are purely visual — GAJOE's fitted scaling constants live in the `EOMfitScaling` RAW workspace and are **not** re-applied here. Any vertical offset between the two curves in this panel is a display artifact of GAJOE's internal normalization, not a physical discrepancy.

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L4-L6), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L11-L13), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L30-L45)

### Panel 2 — Kratky Plot (q²I(q) vs q)

The upper subplot of the stacked figure applies the conventional Kratky transform: both the experimental and fitted series are multiplied point-wise by q² (`expData(:,1).^2.*expData(:,2)` and `crysolEOM(:,1).^2.*crysolEOM(:,2)`). Crucially, the experimental error bars are transformed identically — σ becomes q²·σ — so the uncertainty envelope widens with q rather than staying flat, correctly representing how noise propagates under the Kratky weighting. The q-range and accent color are inherited unchanged from Panel 1.

Interpretively, this transform is the diagnostic heart of the workflow for intrinsically disordered proteins. A compact, globular particle produces a bell-shaped Kratky peak that decays toward the baseline, while a flexible/disordered chain yields a monotonic rise or extended plateau at high q. Agreement between the gray experimental Kratky curve and the orange ensemble Kratky curve in this representation is much more discriminating than the raw I(q) overlay, because q²-weighting amplifies exactly the mid-to-high-q region where conformational differences manifest.

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L47-L64), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L59-L60)

### Panel 3 — Residuals with Error Band

The lower subplot quantifies fit quality as the point-wise difference `I_exp − I_theor`, and its construction involves a subtle but important alignment step: the two input files sit on **different q-grids**, so the script interpolates the experimental intensity and its errors onto the theoretical curve's grid before subtracting. The residual is then drawn as a connected dot sequence, a gray semi-transparent `patch` band shows the ±σ(q) envelope around zero, and a thick black dashed line marks the zero level. The vertical window is fixed at `ylim_residuals = [-1E-2 1E-2]`.

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L66-L83), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L86-L97)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["expData: q_exp, I_exp, σ (raw .dat grid)"] -->|"interp1(q_exp → q_fit)"| B["I_exp aligned, σ aligned"]
    C["crysolEOM: q_fit, I_fit"] --> D["residuals = I_exp_aligned − I_fit"]
    B --> D
    D --> E["plot residuals (o-)"]
    B --> F["patch band: ±σ around zero"]
    E --> G["dashed zero line, ylim ±1e-2"]
    F --> G
```

> [!TIP]
> Note the interpolation *direction*: the experimental data is resampled onto the theoretical grid (`interp1(expData(:,1), expData(:,2), xPoints_crysol)`), never the reverse. This guarantees residuals are evaluated exactly at the q-positions where GAJOE's ensemble profile is defined, and it also means the residual count equals the number of rows in the `.fit` file, not the `.dat` file. Additionally, line 86 zeroes out any `NaN` produced by extrapolation beyond the experimental q-range — `expErrs_interp_crysol(isnan(expErrs_interp_crysol)) = 0` — so the error band does not collapse or crash when the theoretical grid extends past the measured data.

## Configuration Surface

The script's customization points are deliberately minimal — a folder path, a color triple, and two axis-limit vectors — making it straightforward to repoint at a different force field's GA run or the H4KQ variant:

| Parameter | Default | Purpose | Adaptation example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `folder` | `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1` | Location of the GAJOE `.fit` output | Point at a different `GA00X/curve_Y` run directory |
| `theColour` | `[238 68 0]/255` (orange, H4WT) | Accent color for fit curve and residuals | Switch to the commented `[46 80 122]/255` navy for H4KQ |
| `expData` filename | `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat` | Raw experimental profile with σ | Swap to `H4KQ_150Na.dat` for the mutant |
| `xlim_SAXS` | `[0 0.3]` Å⁻¹ | Shared q-window across all panels | Widen/narrow to focus on a q-region of interest |
| `ylim_residuals` | `[-1E-2 1E-2]` | Fixed vertical scale for the residual panel | Adjust to the noise magnitude of your detector |

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L20), [SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat#L1)

## Interpreting the Output

Reading the three panels together yields a compact fit-quality verdict. A sound ensemble fit shows the orange I_fit curve threading the gray error bars in Panel 1, matching Kratky behavior in Panel 2, and — most tellingly — residuals in Panel 3 that scatter *within* the gray ±σ band with no long-wavelength structure. Systematic, slowly-varying residual excursions outside the band (rather than white noise) indicate the ensemble is missing a conformational population — e.g., insufficient compaction or extension sampling in the RANCH pool, which is the input concern governed by [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation). The reported `Chi^2: 1.226` in the `.fit` header (cycle 29 of 100 GA cycles) provides the scalar companion to these visual diagnostics; how that best cycle is selected from the full GA trajectory is covered in [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles).

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L76-L95), [profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1)

## Where to Go Next

This page closes the MATLAB analysis loop: inputs come from GAJOE fitting, and the outputs are purely visual. To understand how `profiles_001_1.fit` was produced, proceed to [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) and the [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference). To see how the best cycle feeding this `.fit` file was reconstructed from `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` logs, read [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles). For a Python-based companion that plots experimental curves and derived distributions, see [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots); the biological interpretation of the H4WT vs. H4KQ comparison this script supports is developed in [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).


# SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots



`graph.py` is the Python plotting utility that transforms a completed GAJOE fit into four publication-ready figures: one **SAXS fit overlay** (experimental data vs. genetic-algorithm ensemble fit) and three **structural distribution plots** (R<sub>g</sub>, D<sub>max</sub>, R<sub>ee</sub>). The script is deliberately minimal — roughly 60 lines, two dependencies, one editable path — making it an ideal first step for beginners who want to visually inspect EOM results before deeper quantitative analysis. This page explains what the script reads, how it parses GAJOE's mixed text/numeric files, how each figure is constructed, and how to customize or troubleshoot it.

This page covers only `graph.py`. Its sibling script `2d.py` (the R<sub>g</sub>–R<sub>ee</sub> scatter plot) is documented in [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals), and the underlying GAJOE fitting process is covered in [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L1-L62), [README.md](README.md#L100-L118)

## Where graph.py Fits in the EOM Workflow

In the repository's tutorial, `graph.py` is invoked at **step 4 ("Plot the results")**, after the three-step ATSAS chain (RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE) has produced a `GA001` output folder. The script consumes GAJOE's output files directly — it never touches the raw MD pool or the experimental `.dat` file again — so it can be re-run instantly after any new GAJOE fit. This makes it the fastest feedback loop in the pipeline: change GAJOE parameters, re-fit, re-plot.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["RANCH<br/>conformational pool"] --> B["FFMAKER<br/>theoretical SAXS profiles"]
    B --> C["GAJOE<br/>GA ensemble fitting"]
    C --> D["GAJOE output folder<br/>GA001/curve_1/"]
    D --> E["graph.py<br/><b>this page</b><br/>SAXS fit + 3 distributions"]
    D --> F["2d.py<br/>Rg-Ree scatter with marginals"]
    D --> G["MATLAB scripts<br/>averaged profiles, Kratky, JSD"]
```

The MATLAB scripts `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` and `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` operate on the same GAJOE outputs but serve deeper analysis (ensemble-averaged profiles, Kratky plots, Jensen-Shannon divergence) — those are covered in [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals) and [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L118), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L5-L5)

## Dependencies and Setup

The script requires only `numpy` and `matplotlib` from PyPI, plus `pathlib` from the standard library. Installation and execution are two commands:

| Item | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Python 3 | Standard-library `pathlib` for file discovery |
| Third-party packages | `numpy`, `matplotlib` | `pip install numpy matplotlib` |
| User-editable setting | `folder = Path("GA001/curve_1")` (line 5) | Must point at your GAJOE output directory |
| Run context | From the directory containing `GA001/` | The path in line 5 is **relative** |

Note the single configuration point: line 5 hard-codes the GAJOE output location as a relative path. The README instructs you to "set the GAJOE output directory in both scripts" before running — this is the line to edit. If you followed the tutorial and ran GAJOE inside `Example_tutorial/`, the default value already works.

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L1-L5), [README.md](README.md#L102-L113)

## Inputs: The Four GAJOE Files It Reads

The script discovers its inputs by **glob patterns** rather than fixed filenames, so it adapts to GAJOE's numbered output naming (`profiles_001_1.fit`, `Rg_distr_001_1.dat`, …). Four patterns drive the entire script:

| Glob pattern (line 40–43 / 24) | Physical quantity | X-axis label | Output figure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `profiles_*.fit` | Experimental I(q) + fitted ensemble I(q) | q (Å⁻¹) vs. I(q), log scale | `saxs_fit.png` |
| `Rg_distr_*.dat` | Radius of gyration distribution | R<sub>g</sub> (Å) | `rg.png` |
| `Size_distr_*.dat` | Maximum particle dimension distribution | D<sub>max</sub> (Å) | `dmax.png` |
| `CaCa_distr_*.dat` | End-to-end (Cα–Cα) distance distribution | R<sub>ee</sub> (Å) | `ree.png` |

Understanding the two file formats explains everything the script does:

**The `.fit` file** starts with a one-line text header — `CYCLE: 29  Chi^2: 1.226  GENER.:1000  ENSEMBLES: 50  CURVES: 9` — followed by rows of four numeric columns: q (Å⁻¹), experimental I(q), experimental error, and the fitted I(q). The script's parser skips the header automatically and reads columns 1–4 in that order.

**The distribution files** carry five header lines (average R<sub>g</sub> of the ensemble vs. pool, plus a column legend) followed by a value/frequency matrix: column 1 holds bin values, and each subsequent column is a frequency curve — typically **Pool freq.** (the full RANCH pool) and **Sel. freq.** (the GAJOE-selected ensemble). Comparing these two curves is the entire point of the distribution plots: it shows which region of conformational space the genetic algorithm promoted.

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L24-L44), [profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1-L4), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L9), [README.md](README.md#L91-L98)

## The Tolerant Numeric Parser: `read_numeric`

GAJOE output files mix descriptive text headers with whitespace-separated numeric bodies, so the script's first building block is a **forgiving parser** (lines 7–21) instead of `numpy.loadtxt`. Its logic, line by line:

1. **Split lines and tokenize** — each line is split on whitespace, with commas first replaced by spaces (line 11), handling both `1.5, 2.3` and `1.5  2.3` styles.
2. **Skip anything non-numeric** — a `ValueError` during float conversion causes the line to be silently dropped via `continue` (lines 12–13). This is precisely how the five-line R<sub>g</sub> header and the `CYCLE:` header vanish without special-casing.
3. **Enforce a minimum column count** — `min_cols` (3 for distributions, 4 for the fit) rejects truncated lines (line 14).
4. **Rectangularize the array** — rows are truncated to the *minimum* column count found across all rows (`ncols = min(map(len, rows))`, line 20), guaranteeing a clean rectangular NumPy array even when GAJOE files have ragged columns.
5. **Fail loudly on empty input** — if nothing numeric survived, a descriptive `ValueError` names the offending file (lines 17–18).

For a beginner, the takeaway is that this parser lets the rest of the script treat GAJOE files as plain matrices: `data[:, :4]` slices the fit file into `q, exp, err, fit` with a single unpacking line (line 27).

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L7-L27)

## Module 1: The SAXS Fit Plot (lines 23–37)

The first module visualizes **how well the selected ensemble reproduces the experiment** — the central quality check of the entire EOM workflow. The sequence is compact:

```python
f = next(folder.glob("profiles_*.fit"))       # first matching .fit file
data = read_numeric(f, min_cols=4)            # header skipped inside parser
q, exp, err, fit = data[:, :4].T              # transpose → four 1-D arrays
```

Plot construction follows standard scatter-fit conventions: experimental points as `errorbar` (dot markers with y-error bars), the GAJOE fit as a connected line, and — critically for SAXS — a **logarithmic y-axis** (`plt.yscale("log")`), because scattering intensity decays over several orders of magnitude and linear axes would crush the high-q region where structural detail lives. The figure is saved as `saxs_fit.png` at 300 dpi (print quality) after `tight_layout()` trims whitespace.

> [!TIP]
> The header of the `.fit` file is where GAJOE records fit quality — in the bundled example, `Chi^2: 1.226` at `CYCLE: 29` ([profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1)) — but `graph.py` discards it during parsing. After plotting, always open the `.fit` file's first line yourself to record the χ² of the curve you are looking at, and remember that `next(folder.glob(...))` plots only the *first* matching profile when multiple GA runs exist.

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L37)

## Module 2: The Structural Distribution Plots (lines 39–59)

The second module is a **table-driven loop**: a list of `(pattern, xlabel, output)` tuples defines all three distribution figures, and the loop body is shared. This is the pattern to study if you want to add a fourth distribution (for example `Volume_distr_*.dat`, which exists in the bundled example data but is not plotted):

```python
for pattern, xlabel, output in [
    ("Rg_distr_*.dat",   r"$R_g$ ($\AA$)",   "rg.png"),
    ("Size_distr_*.dat", r"$D_{max}$ ($\AA$)", "dmax.png"),
    ("CaCa_distr_*.dat", r"$R_{ee}$ ($\AA$)", "ree.png"),
]:
```

For each match, column 0 becomes the x-axis (the bin values in Å) and **every remaining column is plotted as a separate curve** (lines 52–53), labeled generically as `Column 2`, `Column 3`, … In the bundled example, that means two curves per figure — the full pool distribution and the GA-selected ensemble distribution. Their visual comparison answers the scientific question directly: for the H4 tail example, the selected ensemble's average R<sub>g</sub> (15.27 Å) exceeds the pool's (13.77 Å), so the `Sel. freq.` curve visibly shifts right relative to `Pool freq.` — SAXS selection favors extended conformations.

> [!TIP]
> The glob patterns expect the `.dat` extension, but GAJOE outputs documented in the README (and the files bundled in `ExampleData/`) use `.txt` — e.g. `Rg_distr_001_1.txt`. Because the loop silently `continue`s when no file matches (line 47), you get **no error, just three missing figures**. If your distributions don't appear, change the patterns to `*.txt` or rename the files.

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L39-L59), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L5), [README.md](README.md#L94-L96)

## Execution Flow, Start to Finish

The complete runtime behavior — including the failure branches beginners encounter first — is summarized below:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["python graph.py"] --> P1["folder = GA001/curve_1<br/>(line 5, edit me)"]
    P1 --> P2["next(folder.glob('profiles_*.fit'))"]
    P2 --> P3{"Found a .fit file?"}
    P3 -- "No" --> ERR1["StopIteration — script crashes"]
    P3 -- "Yes" --> P4["read_numeric(min_cols=4)<br/>headers dropped, 4 columns kept"]
    P4 --> P5["errorbar(exp) + line(fit)<br/>log y-scale → saxs_fit.png"]
    P5 --> L1["Loop 3 patterns:<br/>Rg / Size Dmax / CaCa Ree"]
    L1 --> L2{"glob found a file?"}
    L2 -- "No" --> L3["Silent skip — no figure"]
    L2 -- "Yes" --> L4["read_numeric(min_cols=2)<br/>column 0 = bins, rest = curves"]
    L4 --> L5["Plot curves labeled<br/>Column 2, Column 3, …"]
    L5 --> L6["Save rg.png / dmax.png / ree.png"]
    L3 --> L7["plt.show() opens all windows"]
    L6 --> L7
```

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L5-L61)

## Customization Quick Reference

| What to change | Where (line) | Why / effect |
|---|---|---|
| GAJOE output directory | 5 | Point at `GA002`, another protein's run, or an absolute path |
| Distribution file extension | 40–43 | `*.dat` → `*.txt` if your GAJOE writes `.txt` outputs |
| Add a fourth distribution | 40–44 | Add e.g. `("Volume_distr_*.dat", r"Volume", "vol.png")` |
| Curve labels | 53 | Replace generic `Column {j+1}` with `Pool` / `Selected` for readability |
| Fit selection among multiple runs | 24 | `sorted(folder.glob(...))[0]` or explicit filename for reproducibility |
| Figure resolution | 37, 59 | `dpi=300` is print-ready; lower for quick drafts |

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L5-L59)

## Troubleshooting for Beginners

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `StopIteration` traceback immediately on start | No `profiles_*.fit` under `folder` — wrong relative path or script run from the wrong directory | Edit line 5 to the correct path; run from a directory that actually contains `GA001/` |
| SAXS fit appears, but no `rg.png` / `dmax.png` / `ree.png` | Extension mismatch: script globs `*.dat`, files are `.txt` (default silent skip) | Change glob patterns on lines 40–43, or rename files |
| `ValueError: No numeric data found in …` | File matched the glob but contains no parseable numeric rows | Verify the file is a GAJOE output and not empty |
| "Column 2"/"Column 3" labels are confusing | Generic auto-labels for each frequency column | Patch line 53 with meaningful names; for the standard two-column case these are Pool and Selected frequencies |
| Fit curve looks different from a colleague's plot | `next(glob)` picked a different cycle's `.fit` when several exist | List `folder.glob("profiles_*.fit")` first and select explicitly |

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L24-L47)

## Next Steps

With your four figures in hand, the natural progression through this repository is: study what each GAJOE output file contains in [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference), then move to the sibling Python script [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals) to see how selected conformations compare against the full pool in 2D, and finally graduate to the MATLAB quantitative tools in [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals) — which extend the fit visualization shown here with Kratky plots and residual analysis. To see these plots applied to real scientific conclusions, continue to the [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).


# Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals



This page documents `Example_tutorial/2d.py`, the Python script that produces the repository's two-dimensional structural ensemble view: a scatter plot of radius of gyration ($R_g$) versus end-to-end distance ($R_{ee}$), decorated with marginal histograms. The plot answers a single, important question visually: *where in conformational space did the EOM genetic algorithm (GAJOE) pick its structures from, compared to the full generated pool?* You only need `numpy` and `matplotlib` to run it — no SAXS knowledge or ATSAS installation is required for this step.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L115-L116), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L2-L5)

## What the Plot Shows and Why It Matters

In ensemble-optimization analysis, you start with a large pool of random conformations and let GAJOE select a small SAXS-consistent subset. If the selection is meaningful, the selected structures should *not* look like a random sample of the pool — they should cluster in a specific region of structural space. The scatter plot makes this visible in two dimensions at once: $R_{ee}$ (how stretched the chain is, x-axis) and $R_g$ (how compact it is, y-axis). The two marginal histograms then collapse each dimension separately, showing the distribution of each quantity alone — a standard joint-plot pattern that lets you judge both the correlation and the individual distributions in one figure.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L58-L71), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L77-L95)

The script distinguishes two groups in the same figure:

| Group | Source of truth | Visual encoding |
|---|---|---|
| **Full pool** | Every row of the FFMAKER size-statistics file | Small solid coral dots (`s=20`, `alpha=0.7`) |
| **Selected by EOM** | CIF files in the GAJOE output `pdbs/` folder | Larger open circles with dodgerblue edges (`s=65`, `linewidths=1.5`) |

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L59-L71)

## Where the Data Comes From and How It Is Joined

The script consumes exactly two inputs, both configured as `pathlib.Path` objects near the top of the file. The first is `size_statistics_20.csv`, produced by FFMAKER, which stores one row per pool conformation with its structural properties ($R_g$, $D_{max}$, $R_{ee}$, volume, and the file name). The second is the GAJOE results directory `GA001/curve_1/pdbs/`, which contains the CIF structures GAJOE chose for the fitted ensemble.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L9), [README.md](README.md#L52-L58)

The parser reads this whitespace-separated file defensively: lines with fewer than six tokens (blank lines, headers) are skipped, column 0 becomes $R_g$, column 2 becomes $R_{ee}$, and column 5 is converted to a bare file name via `Path(p[5]).stem`. The "join" between the two data sources happens through these names: the script builds a set of stems from every `*.cif` file in the `pdbs/` folder and computes a boolean `mask` marking which pool rows were selected.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L14-L34)

Before plotting, the script runs a lightweight integrity audit: it prints the pool size, the number of selected structures, and their names, then asserts that every selected CIF was actually found in the pool statistics. This assertion is your first line of defense against silent data mismatches.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L36-L41)

> [!TIP]
> The pool↔selection join relies entirely on matching file-name stems. If any CIF in `GA001/curve_1/pdbs/` was renamed after GAJOE ran, the stem lookup fails — and the `assert` on line 40 stops the script with *"Some selected structures were not found in the pool!"* rather than plotting a subset that looks deceptively complete.

The complete data flow is summarized below. The diagram assumes you have already run the ATSAS tutorial steps: RANCH generated the pool, FFMAKER computed the statistics, and GAJOE produced the `GA001` results folder.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FFMAKER output<br/>size_statistics_20.csv<br/>(Rg, ..., Ree, ..., name)"] --> C["Parse loop<br/>skips lines with < 6 tokens"]
    C --> D["rg / ree / names arrays"]
    B["GAJOE output<br/>GA001/curve_1/pdbs/*.cif"] --> E["selected_names set<br/>(CIF file stems)"]
    D --> F["Boolean mask:<br/>name in selected_names"]
    E --> F
    F --> G{"assert selected<br/>all found in pool"}
    G --> H["GridSpec figure:<br/>scatter + 2 marginals"]
    H --> I["EOM_2D.png<br/>(300 dpi)"]
```

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L11-L41), [README.md](README.md#L38-L98)

## Figure Layout: A GridSpec Joint Plot

Rather than relying on seaborn's `jointplot`, the script builds the classic three-panel layout manually with `matplotlib.gridspec.GridSpec`, which gives you full control with only the base matplotlib install. A 7×6 inch figure is divided into a 2×2 grid where the bottom-left cell is the tall, wide main scatter panel; the top-left cell holds the $R_{ee}$ histogram; and the bottom-right cell holds the horizontal $R_g$ histogram. The top-right cell is deliberately left empty.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L44-L56)

| Grid cell | Axes variable | Content | Axis sharing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[1, 0]` (bottom-left) | `ax` | $R_{ee}$ vs $R_g$ scatter | — |
| `[0, 0]` (top-left) | `ax_top` | $R_{ee}$ histogram | `sharex=ax` |
| `[1, 1]` (bottom-right) | `ax_right` | $R_{eg}$ histogram, horizontal | `sharey=ax` |
| `[0, 1]` (top-right) | *(unused)* | empty | — |

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L46-L56)

Two layout details do the quiet work here. First, the width/height ratios (`[4, 1.3]` and `[1.3, 4]`) and the small spacing (`hspace=0.05`, `wspace=0.05`) pack the marginals tightly against the scatter, producing the seamless joint-plot look. Second, because the marginal axes *share* axes with the scatter, their limits stay synchronized with the data automatically — and the script then hides their tick labels (`labelbottom=False`, `labelleft=False`) to avoid duplicated numbers between panels.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L46-L52), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L103-L104)

## Marginal Histograms: Making Pool and Selection Comparable

Each marginal is actually **two overlaid histograms**: the full pool in translucent coral and the selected subset in translucent dodgerblue, plotted with identical bin edges and `density=True`. Density normalization converts raw counts into a probability density, which is essential here because the pool may contain hundreds of structures while the selected ensemble has far fewer — without it, the selected histogram would be nearly invisible next to the pool's. The top panel bins $R_{ee}$ values; the right panel bins $R_g$ values with `orientation="horizontal"` so the bars grow toward the scatter's y-axis.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L74-L95)

The bin edges are generated with `np.linspace(0, max(value) * 1.1, 12)`: twelve evenly spaced edge values starting at 0 and extending 10% past the largest data point, which yields equal-width bins covering the full data range plus headroom. Because both overlaid histograms in a panel receive the *same* edges array, the comparison is apples-to-apples.

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L74-L75)

> [!TIP]
> `density=True` plus identical bin edges is the entire statistical contract of the marginals. If you customize the script, change `bins_ree`/`bins_rg` for both overlaid histograms together — giving the pool and the selection different binning would silently distort the visual comparison, since bar heights would no longer be on the same density scale.

## Running and Customizing the Script

The standard workflow (from the repository's EOM tutorial) is to install the two dependencies, point the script at your GAJOE results, and run it from the `Example_tutorial` directory. The script writes its figure to `EOM_2D.png` at 300 dpi with tight bounding box, then opens an interactive window via `plt.show()`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L102-L113), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L106-L107)

```bash
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib
# edit size_file and selected_dir in 2d.py first
python 2d.py
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L104-L113)

The two knobs you must always set for your own data:

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `size_file` | `size_statistics_20.csv` | FFMAKER size-statistics file for your pool |
| `selected_dir` | `GA001/curve_1/pdbs` | GAJOE output folder holding selected CIFs |

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L9)

Common customization points, all localized to a few lines:

| What you want to change | Where in `2d.py` | How |
|---|---|---|
| Point size / highlight ring | lines 59–71 | adjust `s`, `linewidths`, `alpha` |
| Histogram resolution | lines 74–75 | change the `12` in `np.linspace` (edges) |
| Colors | lines 59–95 | replace `"coral"` / `"dodgerblue"` |
| Axis labels & font size | lines 98–99 | edit the `r"$R_{ee}$ ($\AA$)"` strings |
| Output filename / resolution | line 106 | change `"EOM_2D.png"` / `dpi` |

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L59-L107)

Troubleshooting quick reference, grounded in the script's actual behavior:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `AssertionError: Some selected structures were not found in the pool!` | CIF files renamed, or `selected_dir` points to the wrong `GA*` run | keep GAJOE's original names; verify the path |
| Both `Pool:` and `Selected by GAJOE:` print `0` / empty plot | statistics file is comma-separated (the parser splits on whitespace only) | convert commas to spaces/tabs first |
| `IndexError` or empty arrays on load | `size_file` path wrong, so the parser skipped every line | check the CSV exists relative to your working directory |
| Marginal histograms look misaligned with scatter | axes-sharing lines removed during editing | restore `sharex=` / `sharey=` in the `add_subplot` calls |

Sources: [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L14-L22), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L40-L41), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L54-L56)

## How 2d.py Fits in the Repository's Plotting Toolbox

This script is the Python counterpart in a family of ensemble-comparison tools. It complements rather than replaces them: `graph.py` (same folder) plots the SAXS fit and 1D structural distributions from GAJOE text outputs, while the MATLAB scripts operate on the full-scale H4 benchmarking data in `ExampleData/`.

| Tool | Language | Input | Output | Catalog page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Example_tutorial/2d.py` | Python | FFMAKER CSV + GAJOE `pdbs/` | `EOM_2D.png` joint scatter | this page |
| `Example_tutorial/graph.py` | Python | GAJOE `.fit` / `*_distr_*.dat` files | SAXS fit + 1D distribution PNGs | [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots) |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | MATLAB | GA cycle files, `Size_list.txt` | 2D histograms + JS divergence | [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms) |

Sources: [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L23-L59), [README.md](README.md#L15-L17), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L9)
