# Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree



This page explains the three structural descriptors — **radius of gyration (Rg)**, **maximum dimension (Dmax)**, and **end-to-end distance (Ree)** — that parameterize every conformation in the H4 tail benchmarking workflow. These descriptors are the bridge between atomistic MD structures and SAXS-refined ensembles: RANCH generates conformations, FFMAKER measures them, GAJOE selects from them, and the MATLAB/Python scripts in this repository visualize and quantify how the selected ensemble's descriptor distributions shift relative to the full MD pool. You will learn what each descriptor measures, exactly which files store it, and how the analysis scripts read, weight, and compare it. This page assumes you have completed the [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools) and understand the pipeline at the level of [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L17), [README.md](README.md#L56-L60)

## Why Three Descriptors Define an IDP Ensemble

Intrinsically disordered proteins like the 26-residue H4 tail (`assignment.txt` declares it `disordered`, and `protein.seq` provides the sequence `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`) cannot be summarized by a single static structure. Instead, each conformation in the pool is reduced to a compact geometric fingerprint: **Rg** captures overall compactness (mass-weighted spread around the center of mass), **Dmax** captures the longest linear extent within the molecule, and **Ree** captures the span between the chain's first and last Cα atoms. Together they distinguish compact, globule-like, and extended conformations that SAXS measurements are sensitive to. The example data makes this concrete: the pool's average Rg is 13.77 Å while the SAXS-selected ensemble's average Rg rises to 15.27 Å — a compaction-versus-extension signature that is the central readout of the entire pipeline.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Conformation["One PDB/CIF conformation"]
        A["All atom coordinates"]
    end
    A -->|"mass-weighted spread about center of mass"| Rg["Rg (Å)<br/>compactness"]
    A -->|"largest intra-molecular pair distance"| Dmax["Dmax (Å)<br/>max linear extent"]
    A -->|"Cα(first) to Cα(last) distance"| Ree["Ree (Å)<br/>chain end-to-end span"]
    Rg & Dmax & Ree --> F["Geometric fingerprint<br/>one row per conformation"]
```

Prerequisite for the diagram: each box is a scalar derived directly from Cartesian coordinates; a single conformation yields one triple (Rg, Dmax, Ree), and a pool of N conformations yields N triples — the raw material for every distribution plot downstream.

Sources: [assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L4), [Size_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L4)

## Descriptor Data Flow Through the EOM Pipeline

The descriptors originate in the ATSAS tools and terminate in this repository's analysis scripts. The flow below shows where each descriptor is born and where it is consumed — this is the pattern to keep in mind when debugging "missing descriptor" errors.

```mermaid
graph TD
    R["RANCH<br/>(random conformations)"] -->|"*.cif / *.pdb"| FF["FFMAKER<br/>(per-conformation geometry)"]
    FF -->|"size_statistics_20.csv<br/>Rg, Dmax, Ree, volume"| G["GAJOE<br/>(genetic algorithm selection)"]
    FF -->|"theoretical I(q) profiles"| G
    G -->|"Size_list.txt: Rg, Dmax"| M["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>Rg-Ree and Rg-Dmax figures,<br/>mean ± SEM, JSD"]
    G -->|"Rg_distr / Size_distr / CaCa_distr"| P1["graph.py<br/>pool vs. selected distributions"]
    G -->|"pdbs/ selected CIFs"| P2["2d.py<br/>Rg-Ree scatter + marginals"]
    E["pdb_Rmeas.m (external)<br/>Ree_values.mat"] --> M
    M -.->|"best_curve via getBestCurve"| M2["getBestCurve.m"]
```

Prerequisite for the diagram: solid arrows are file outputs produced by the named tool; the dashed arrow is an in-process function call; the external box covers the one descriptor (Ree) that GAJOE v2.1 does **not** populate in this workflow.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L98), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L30-L39), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L39-L59), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L8-L9)

## On-Disk Formats: Where Each Descriptor Lives

Each descriptor has one "per-conformation" home and one "distribution" home. The per-conformation records feed scatter plots and mean calculations; the distribution records are GAJOE's own binned histograms of pool versus selected frequencies. The verified formats, using the shipped example data (a 2000-conformation pool), are:

| File | Producer | Columns / content | Descriptor(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Size_list.txt` | GAJOE | col 1 = conformation index, col 2 = Rg, col 3 = Dmax (2000 rows, no header) | Rg, Dmax |
| `size_statistics_20.csv` (FFMAKER) | FFMAKER | col 1 = Rg, col 3 = Ree, col 6 = conformation name (Dmax and volume in cols 2, 4) | Rg, Dmax, Ree |
| `Rg_distr_001_1.txt` | GAJOE | 4 summary header lines, then Rg \| Pool freq. \| Sel. freq. | Rg distribution |
| `Size_distr_001_1.txt` | GAJOE | 4 summary header lines, then Size \| Pool freq. \| Sel. freq. | Dmax distribution |
| `CaCa_distr_001_1.txt` | GAJOE | same layout, but all zeros in this example dataset | Ree distribution (unpopulated) |
| `Ree_values.mat` | `pdb_Rmeas.m` (run externally) | MATLAB variable `R` — one Ree per pool conformation | Ree |

The four header lines of each `*_distr` file are themselves a compact summary report: for example, `Rg_distr_001_1.txt` states *Ense Average Rg = 15.27*, *Ense Histogram Rg = 15.15*, *Pool Average Rg = 13.77*, *Pool Histogram Rg = 13.64*, and `Size_distr_001_1.txt` states *Ense Average Dmax = 47.33* versus *Pool Average Dmax = 42.69* — quantifying the ensemble's expansion relative to the pool before you plot anything.

Sources: [Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L15), [Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1996-L2000), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L12-L24), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L6), [Size_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L7), [CaCa_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/CaCa_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L5), [README.md](README.md#L56-L60)

## Reading Descriptors in MATLAB and Python

The two language stacks use different parsing conventions for the same descriptors, and knowing both is essential because the repository's full-featured analysis is MATLAB while the quick tutorial is Python. In MATLAB, `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` loads Ree from `Ree_values.mat` (variable `R`) and imports `Size_list.txt` with `importdata`, then projects columns into a `pool` struct (`pool.dmax = Sizelist(:,3)`, `pool.rg = Sizelist(:,2)`, `pool.r = R(1:end)`). In Python, `2d.py` streams the FFMAKER CSV line by line, skipping short lines, and maps whitespace-split fields positionally: field 0 → `rg`, field 2 → `ree`, field 5 → structure name. `graph.py` takes a more defensive approach — its `read_numeric` helper tries to cast every whitespace-separated token to `float` and silently skips header lines that fail, which is why it can consume GAJOE's mixed header/distribution files unchanged.

| Aspect | MATLAB path (`make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`) | Python path (`2d.py` / `graph.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| Descriptor source file | `Size_list.txt` + `Ree_values.mat` | `size_statistics_20.csv` |
| Column mapping | col 2 → Rg, col 3 → Dmax, `.mat` → Ree | field 1 → Rg, field 3 → Ree, field 6 → name |
| Ree handling | loaded from external `Ree_values.mat` | read directly from FFMAKER CSV |
| Header handling | `importdata` / `.mat` load | skip short lines; float-cast try/except |

> [!TIP]
> The `CaCa_distr_001_1.txt` shipped in the example data is **entirely zeros** — GAJOE v2.1 did not compute Cα–Cα distances for this pool. That is why the MATLAB script never reads that file for Ree and instead requires a separately generated `Ree_values.mat` (see the script's header comment referencing `pdb_Rmeas.m`, a helper outside this repository). If your Ree histograms look degenerate, check this file first.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L39), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L1-L9), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L12-L24), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L7-L21)

## Weighting the Selected Ensemble

A subtle but decisive detail: the GA-selected "ensemble" is not a list of structures — it is a list of structure *occupancies*. `getBestCurve.m` parses all `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files across the requested number of GA runs (`nRuns`), takes the last `curvesPerEnsemble` numeric rows of each (the selected structures), concatenates everything, and tabulates selection frequencies into a two-column result `[PDB number, frequency]`. `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` then **expands** each selected conformation by repeating its descriptor values `bestcurve(n,2)` times with `repmat`, building weighted arrays `gajoe.dmax`, `gajoe.rg`, and `gajoe.r`. Consequently, the "EOM pool" histograms and scatter points represent occupancy-weighted descriptor distributions — a structure selected in 40 of 100 GA runs contributes 40 copies of its (Rg, Dmax, Ree) triple. This weighting is what makes pool-versus-ensemble comparisons statistically meaningful rather than set-membership counts.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L19-L39), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L45-L55), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L16)

## Summarizing Ensembles: Mean ± Standard Error

After weighting, the script prints a uniform summary statistic for each descriptor: the mean and the standard error of the mean, computed identically for the full MD pool and the GA-selected ensemble — `mean(x)` and `std(x)./sqrt(numel(x))` for Rg (active) and Ree (active), with the Dmax block present but commented out. This mirrors the average-vs-histogram distinction in GAJOE's own distribution headers (mean of raw values versus mean of binned histogram), and in the example data both methods agree closely (Rg ensemble average 15.27 Å vs. histogram 15.15 Å). When benchmarking force fields — the purpose of this repository — this pool-vs-ensemble delta is the primary quantitative signal, e.g., a SAXS-refined ensemble shifting toward larger Rg and Dmax indicates the experiment favors more extended conformations than the raw MD pool provides.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L116-L130), [Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L4), [Size_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L4)

## From Descriptors to Quantitative Comparison: Jensen-Shannon Divergence

Means are blunt instruments; the repository also compares the *full shapes* of descriptor distributions using the **Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD)** between the MD pool and the SAXS-refined ensemble. The implementation (added September 2025, adapted from RNA-condensate analysis tooling) is compact: both descriptor arrays are binned with the same fixed bin count (22 bins for Rg and Ree), converted to probability density functions via `histcounts(...,'Normalization','pdf')`, and JSD is assembled from a Shannon entropy helper `H(p) = -sum(p.*log(p))` as `JSD = H(0.5p₁+0.5p₂) − 0.5H(p₁) − 0.5H(p₂)`. The helper guards against the degenerate `0·log(0)` case by replacing `NaN` entries with 0. JSD is computed independently for Rg (`JSD_rg`) and Ree (`JSD_r`), returning values in nats that approach 0 when the distributions are indistinguishable — this is the number that says whether SAXS selection actually reshaped the ensemble's geometry. For a deeper treatment of the entropy machinery, see [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification).

> [!TIP]
> Note the two different normalizations in this script: display histograms are normalized so the tallest bin equals 1 (`.BinCounts = .../max(...)`), while JSD histograms use proper PDF normalization. Reusing the display-normalized counts in an entropy calculation would silently corrupt the result — always reach for the `'Normalization','pdf'` variants when comparing distributions.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L206), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L209-L234), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L92-L110)

## Visualizing Descriptor Space

The descriptors are rendered in two complementary 2D projections, both in MATLAB and Python. The **Rg–Ree plane** is the workhorse: the MATLAB version (`make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`) draws the full pool as orange dots and the occupancy-weighted selected ensemble as blue open circles over fixed axes (`xlim_R = [0 80]`, `ylim_Rg = [5 30]`), flanked by normalized marginal histograms of Ree (top) and Rg (right, axis-reversed via `camroll(-90)`); the Python version (`2d.py`) reproduces the same layout with matplotlib `GridSpec` by masking the pool arrays against the CIF filenames found in `GA001/curve_1/pdbs`. The **Rg–Dmax plane** (`xlim_Dmax = [20 80]`) is the MATLAB-only second figure, useful because Dmax is the descriptor most directly constrained by the SAXS P(r) function, whereas Ree probes internal chain architecture that SAXS alone cannot resolve. Additionally, `graph.py` plots the raw pool-vs-selected frequency curves for all three descriptors from the `*_distr` files. Full walkthroughs of these figures live in [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms), [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals), and [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots).

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L58-L111), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L18-L26), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L134-L180), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L27-L95), [graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L39-L59), [README.md](README.md#L115-L117)

## How the Three Descriptors Cooperate

The descriptors are deliberately redundant — each is blind to a pathology the others catch. The concept map below summarizes their complementary roles in validating an ensemble:

| Descriptor | Sensitive to | Blind to | Primary producer | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rg | Global compactness | Internal asymmetry, chain closure | FFMAKER / GAJOE (`Size_list.txt`) | JSD, mean ± SEM, both scatter plots |
| Dmax | Longest extent (SAXS P(r) constraint) | Where mass sits within that extent | FFMAKER / GAJOE (`Size_list.txt`) | Rg–Dmax figure, mean block |
| Ree | Chain end-to-end architecture | Mass distribution along the chain | `pdb_Rmeas.m` → `Ree_values.mat` (MATLAB) / FFMAKER CSV (Python) | Rg–Ree figure, JSD, mean ± SEM |

Practical consequence: a compact-but-bent conformation can have small Rg yet large Ree; an extended-but-folded-back chain can have large Dmax yet modest Ree. Only the joint (Rg, Dmax, Ree) fingerprint disambiguates these cases, which is why the pipeline never relies on a single descriptor.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L36-L39), [2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L14-L24), [README.md](README.md#L58-L58)

## Practical Checklist and Next Steps

When working with your own GAJOE output, verify the descriptor chain end-to-end before plotting: confirm `Size_list.txt` has one row per pool conformation (the example has 2000), confirm `Ree_values.mat` exists and contains variable `R` with matching length, set `nRuns` and `curvesPerEnsemble` to the values you entered in GAJOE, and adjust the axes limits (`xlim_Dmax`, `ylim_Rg`, `xlim_R`) and bin counts to your protein's size range. To understand where these descriptor files come from, read [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation) and [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles); for the complete inventory of GAJOE output files beyond descriptors, see [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference); to see how descriptor shifts drive biological conclusions for the histone H4 tail, continue to [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).


# H4 Histone Tail Case Study



This page is the Deep Dive capstone of the documentation: it explains how every pipeline component documented so far — RANCH pool generation, FFMAKER profile computation, GAJOE ensemble fitting, and the MATLAB/Python analysis scripts — converges on one concrete scientific problem. The repository ships a complete, reproducible instance of this problem: the wild-type (WT) H4 histone tail, simulated in solution and benchmarked against experimental small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data, alongside its charge-neutralized K-to-Q mutant for comparison. If you have followed the mechanics pages, this case study shows them working together on real data.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L19)

## Scientific Context: What Is Being Benchmarked

The case study originates from the paper *Combining atomistic simulation and solution scattering to reveal charge-driven histone H4 tail conformational changes* (Wang, Kolesnikov, Pollack, Onufriev, 2026, in submission), which this repository accompanies. The central scientific question is whether atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) ensembles of the intrinsically disordered H4 tail reproduce solution scattering measurements — and how the ensemble shifts when positive charges on the tail are neutralized by lysine-to-glutamine (K-to-Q) substitution. The folder naming `H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC` encodes the simulation provenance directly: the AMBER `ff19SB` protein force field with `OPC` water, produced with AMBER 24 as stated in the software notes.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["H4 tail: 12 basic residues<br/>(K/R)"] -->|K-to-Q mutation| B["Charge-neutralized<br/>H4KQ variant"]
    A --> C["MD ensemble<br/>AMBER 24, ff19SB + OPC"]
    B --> D["Experimental SAXS<br/>H4KQ_150Na.dat"]
    C --> E["Experimental SAXS<br/>H4WT_150Na.dat"]
    C --> F["EOM/GAJOE refinement"]
    F --> G["Compare ensembles:<br/>does MD match solution?"]
    E --> G
    B --> H["MD ensemble shift?"]
    H --> G
```

The benchmark logic is symmetric in both directions: SAXS validates whether the MD ensemble is physically realistic, and the MD ensemble provides residue-level structural interpretation for what SAXS measures indirectly. This two-way relationship is what makes the H4 tail a case study rather than a mere example — it is the evidentiary core of the associated paper.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L19), [README.md](README.md#L113-L114)

## The Molecule: Sequence-Level Definition of the H4 Tail

The H4 tail is defined at the sequence level in `Example_tutorial/protein.seq`: a 26-residue fragment `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`, declared as chain `A` with residues 1–26 marked `disordered` in `assignment.txt`. This two-file pair is exactly what RANCH consumes to generate conformational pools — the `disordered` flag tells RANCH to treat the entire fragment as a flexible chain rather than inheriting secondary structure.

| File | Content | Role in pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| `protein.seq` | FASTA entry `>A` with 26-residue sequence | Defines the chain identity and sequence |
| `assignment.txt` | `A 1 26 disordered` | Declares chain A, residues 1–26, disordered region for RANCH |

Scanning the sequence reveals why this tail is a charge-driven system: it is densely packed with lysine (`K`) and arginine (`R`) residues — roughly half the fragment — including the acetylation-site lysines that the K-to-Q mutation targets. This charge density is the physical basis for the "charge-driven conformational changes" the paper investigates: neutralizing even a subset of these charges alters intramolecular electrostatic repulsion and therefore the tail's conformational distribution.

Sources: [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](assignment.txt#L1-L2)

## Case Study Data Assets

The repository organizes the case study into three directories, each serving a distinct role. `SAXSData/` holds the experimental ground truth, `ExampleData/` holds a complete GAJOE refinement result for the WT tail, and `Example_tutorial/` holds a miniature hands-on reproduction.

| Directory | Contents | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `SAXSData/` | `H4WT_150Na.dat` (53 q-points), `H4KQ_150Na.dat` (56 q-points) | Experimental SAXS profiles at 150 mM NaCl |
| `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/` | 100 `GA_CYCLE` files, `profiles_001_1.fit`, four distribution files, `Size_list.txt`, `Ree_values.mat` | Complete GAJOE v2 output for the WT tail |
| `Example_tutorial/` | `protein.seq`, `assignment.txt`, `H4WT_150Na.dat`, `graph.py`, `2d.py` | Minimal 20-conformation workflow demonstration |

Both experimental files use the standard three-column `.dat` format — q, I(q), error — with a 4-line header; the WT profile begins at q ≈ 0.0156 Å⁻¹ and the KQ profile at q ≈ 0.0199 Å⁻¹. The `150Na` suffix in both filenames records the ionic condition (150 mM NaCl) under which the scattering was measured, which matters because salt screens the very electrostatic interactions under study.

Sources: [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L7), [SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat#L1-L7), [README.md](README.md#L15-L19)

## The Refinement Run: Anatomy of GA001

`ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/` is a saved GAJOE work directory for one genetic-algorithm curve, and its contents reveal the exact optimization settings used for the case study. The first line of `profiles_001_1.fit` states that the best cycle was **cycle 29** with **χ² = 1.226**, run for **1000 generations** across **50 candidate ensembles** with up to **9 curves per ensemble**. The presence of exactly 100 `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files confirms the GA was independently repeated 100 times — matching the `nRuns = 100` setting in the analysis script.

| Artifact | Verified content | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `profiles_001_1.fit` | `CYCLE: 29 Chi^2: 1.226 GENER.: 1000 ENSEMBLES: 50 CURVES: 9` | Best fit achieved; χ² ≈ 1.2 indicates close agreement with experiment |
| `GA_CYCLE_1.txt` … `GA_CYCLE_100.txt` | ~20,000 lines each; records like `-103-329-460-…` list pool structure indices per generation | Full genetic-algorithm trajectory, savable only with GAJOE's "save workfiles" option |
| `Size_list.txt` | 2,000 rows; columns: index, Rg, Dmax | The full MD pool: 2,000 conformations with per-structure sizes |
| `Ree_values.mat` | Vector `R` of end-to-end distances | Computed independently from pool PDBs (see below) |
| `Rg_distr_001_1.txt`, `Size_distr_001_1.txt`, `CaCa_distr_001_1.txt`, `Volume_distr_001_1.txt` | Pool vs. selected frequency distributions | GAJOE's own comparison of full pool against SAXS-selected ensemble |

> [!TIP]
> The end-to-end distances in `Ree_values.mat` are not a native GAJOE output — the header of `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` instructs you to compute R (Ree) over the full pool PDBs first and load the result into the workspace before the 2D plots will run. This is the one manual preprocessing step in the case study.

Sources: [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_29.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_29.txt#L1-L8), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L5), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L3-L6)

## What the Numbers Reveal: A Measurable Ensemble Shift

The distribution files quantify the case study's central observation. In `Rg_distr_001_1.txt`, the **selected ensemble** has average radius of gyration 15.15–15.27 Å, while the **full pool** sits at 13.64–13.77 Å. The SAXS-selected ensemble is thus measurably *more extended* than the raw ff19SB/OPC pool — the genetic algorithm systematically enriched for expanded conformations when fitting the experimental data. This is precisely the kind of MD-versus-solution discrepancy the benchmark exists to expose and quantify.

| Quantity | Full MD pool | SAXS-selected ensemble | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rg (average) | 13.64–13.77 Å | 15.15–15.27 Å | EOM enriches extended conformations |
| Pool size | 2,000 conformations | Frequency-weighted subset | GA selection over 100 runs |
| Fit quality | — | χ² = 1.226 | Theoretical profile matches experiment |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Full MD pool<br/>2,000 conformations<br/>Rg avg ≈ 13.7 Å"] -->|"FFMAKER theoretical profiles"| B["GAJOE genetic algorithm<br/>100 runs × 1000 generations"]
    B -->|"cycle 29, χ² = 1.226"| C["Selected ensemble<br/>Rg avg ≈ 15.2 Å"]
    C --> D{"Ensemble shifted?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Quantify shift:<br/>2D histograms + JSD"]
    A --> E
    E --> F["Benchmark verdict on<br/>ff19SB/OPC for H4 tail"]
```

Sources: [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Rg_distr_001_1.txt#L1-L10), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1)

## Case-Study-Specific Analysis Scripts

Three MATLAB scripts form the case-study analysis layer, and all three are pre-configured to point at this exact dataset. Their user-defined parameters are the only things that need editing when reproducing the analysis on your own GAJOE outputs.

| Script | User-defined parameters (as shipped) | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `getBestCurve.m` | `dir`, `nRuns`, `curvesPerEnsemble` | Frequency table of pool structures selected by the GA |
| `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` | `dir = 'ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1'`, `nRuns = 100`, `curvesPerEnsemble = 20`, axis limits, histogram bins | 2D Rg–Ree and Dmax–Rg scatter plots with marginals, means ± SE, JSD values |
| `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | `folder = 'ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1'`, WT/KQ color selection | SAXS fit overlay, dimensionless Kratky plot, residuals with error band |

`getBestCurve.m` exists to solve a version-compatibility problem: GAJOE v2 removed the `best_curve.txt` file that v1.3 emitted, so this function re-derives it by parsing all 100 `GA_CYCLE` files (delimited by `-`), tabulating which pool structures appear across all final ensembles, and returning `[PDBnum, frequency]` pairs. It only works if GAJOE was run with "Save workfiles with the entire GA runs" answered **yes** — the case study's `GA001` folder demonstrates what that output looks like.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L2-L15), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L20-L43), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L14-L27), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L7-L14)

### Ensemble Comparison and Divergence Quantification

`make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` produces the flagship comparison figure of the case study: the full MD pool plotted as orange points and the EOM-selected ensemble as blue circles in (Rg, Ree) and (Rg, Dmax) space, with normalized marginal histograms added in September 2025. It also prints mean ± standard error for Rg, Dmax, and Ree of both populations — the quantitative summary underlying the ensemble shift table above.

The script then computes the **Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD)** between the pool and selected-ensemble distributions for both Rg and Ree, binning each population as a probability density and evaluating JSD = H(½p₁ + ½p₂) − ½H(p₁) − ½H(p₂) via a local Shannon-entropy subfunction. The method is credited to the RNA condensates software's `plotIterativeAnalysis.m`. A low JSD means GAJOE's selection did not distort the pool distribution (MD matches solution); a high JSD quantifies exactly how far the SAXS-refined ensemble departs from the simulation.

> [!TIP]
> The histograms fed to the JSD use a shared bin count (`binsRg = binsR = 22`), so the divergence value depends on binning choice — keep bins fixed when comparing JSD across systems (e.g., WT vs. KQ) for the number to be meaningful.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L84-L111), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L116-L130), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L234)

### Fit Quality Visualization

`plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` closes the loop by overlaying the GAJOE ensemble profile against the experimental curve, then rendering a Kratky plot (q²I(q) vs. q — the standard IDP diagnostics that emphasizes mid-q deviations from Gaussian-chain behavior) and a residual panel. The residuals are computed by interpolating the experimental I(q) and error onto the CRYSOL q-grid, with the experimental uncertainty shown as a shaded band around zero — so the reader can judge whether deviations are within noise. The script reads `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat` with 4 header lines skipped and `profiles_001_1.fit` with 1, and carries commented color definitions for switching to the KQ dataset (`[46 80 122]/255` in place of the WT orange `[238 68 0]/255`).

Sources: [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L18-L24), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L55-L78), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L78-L103)

## The Comparative Dimension: WT vs. K-to-Q

The case study's scientific punchline lives in the WT-vs-KQ comparison. `SAXSData/` provides both experimental profiles at the same 150 mM NaCl condition, and `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` encodes the intended visualization convention: orange for H4WT, blue for H4KQ. Repeating the full pipeline — pool generation, FFMAKER, GAJOE, and the three MATLAB scripts — on a KQ pool and swapping the dataset references yields directly comparable figures and JSD values between the charged and neutralized tails.

| Dimension | H4WT | H4KQ |
|---|---|---|
| Chemical change | Native lysines (positive) | Selected K → Q (neutral) |
| Experimental data | 53 q-points, q from 0.0156 Å⁻¹ | 56 q-points, q from 0.0199 Å⁻¹ |
| Plot color convention | `[238 68 0]/255` (orange) | `[46 80 122]/255` (blue, commented in script) |
| Role in benchmark | Reference ff19SB/OPC ensemble | Tests whether MD captures charge-driven shifts |

Sources: [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L7), [SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat#L1-L7), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L11-L14)

## Hands-On Miniature: Reproducing the Case Study in 20 Conformations

`Example_tutorial/` packages the entire case-study logic into a runnable miniature: a 20-conformation RANCH pool generated from the same H4 sequence, FFMAKER profiles, and a single quick GAJOE run (1 GA run, 100 generations, ensembles of 1–10 non-repeated conformers) fitted against a local copy of the WT data. The README is explicit that this scale is for workflow demonstration only — quantitative ensemble analysis requires far larger, adequately sampled pools like the shipped 2,000-conformation GA001 pool. The two Python scripts then mirror the MATLAB analysis at small scale: `graph.py` renders the SAXS fit and the Rg/Dmax/Ree distributions from the `GA001/curve_1` folder, while `2d.py` rebuilds the Rg–Ree scatter with marginals by matching `size_statistics_20.csv` rows against the CIF filenames GAJOE placed in `GA001/curve_1/pdbs/`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["protein.seq + assignment.txt<br/>(H4 tail, 26 res, disordered)"] --> R["RANCH<br/>20-conformation pool"]
    R --> F["FFMAKER<br/>intensities + size statistics"]
    F --> G["GAJOE<br/>fit vs H4WT_150Na.dat"]
    G --> O["GA001/curve_1/<br/>fit + distributions + pdbs/"]
    O --> P1["graph.py<br/>SAXS fit + distributions"]
    O --> P2["2d.py<br/>Rg-Ree scatter + marginals"]
```

For the complete command-by-command walkthrough of this miniature — including every GAJOE flag explained — see the dedicated tutorial page [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools); the per-file formats are catalogued in [GAJOE Output File Reference](9-gajoe-output-file-reference).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L68-L78), [Example_tutorial/graph.py](Example_tutorial/graph.py#L12-L42), [Example_tutorial/2d.py](Example_tutorial/2d.py#L7-L39)

The case study touches nearly every other page in this documentation, so here is the recommended traversal depending on your goal:

- **Understand the fitting mechanics** → [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles) and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting).

# MD Ensemble Generation with AMBER



This page documents the upstream stage of the IDP MD–SAXS benchmark: how intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) conformational pools are generated by molecular dynamics in **AMBER** and packaged into the exact artifact formats that the EOM refinement and MATLAB/Python analysis halves of this repository consume. Because the repository ships the *analysis half* of the pipeline rather than simulation scripts, this page separates two layers explicitly: the **repo-verified configuration** of the H4 benchmark, and the **canonical AMBER protocol** needed to reproduce an equivalent pool.

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L8), [README.md](README.md#L22-L25)

## Where the MD Stage Sits in the Architecture

In this benchmark, MD is the **source of physical sampling**. Instead of relying on randomly generated conformers, the full structural pool originates from an atomistic trajectory; EOM then re-weights a SAXS-consistent subset out of that pool. The benchmark signal — what the paper is actually measuring — is the *distance* between the full MD distribution and the SAXS-refined distribution, quantified through 2D histograms and Jensen–Shannon divergence. The full data flow is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph MD["AMBER 24 MD stage"]
        LEaP["System setup<br/>ff19SB + OPC + 150 mM Na"] --> Heat["Minimization & thermalization"]
        Heat --> Prod["Production trajectory"]
    end
    subgraph POOL["Ensemble pool — 2000 frames"]
        Prod --> SNAPS["Full-pool structures<br/>(PDB/CIF)"]
        Prod --> SIZE["Size_list.txt<br/>[frame ID, Rg, Dmax]"]
        Prod --> REE["Ree_values.mat<br/>variable R"]
    end
    subgraph EOM["EOM refinement (ATSAS)"]
        FF["FFMAKER"] --> GA["GAJOE selection"]
        SNAPS --> FF
    end
    subgraph AN["Analysis (this repository)"]
        GA --> BC["GA_CYCLE_*.txt → getBestCurve.m"]
        BC --> CMP["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>full MD pool vs EOM subset"]
        CMP --> JSD["Jensen–Shannon divergence"]
        GA --> FIT["plotEOMSAXScomparison.m<br/>fit / Kratky / residuals"]
    end
    EXP["Experimental SAXS<br/>SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat"] --> GA
    EXP --> FIT
```

The critical architectural fact for anyone extending this workflow: **this repository does not ship AMBER input files**. The README states only that *"Molecular dynamics simulations are run using AMBER 24"*, while everything downstream — pool descriptors, GAJOE outputs, and the comparison scripts — is present and executable. The MD stage is therefore defined here by its *output contract* (see next sections), which the analysis code hard-codes.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L17), [README.md](README.md#L22-L25), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L2-L4)

## Verified Simulation Configuration

Every configuration value below is anchored to repository evidence — the folder naming, data file headers, and pool statistics — rather than to assumption:

| Setting | Value | Evidence basis |
|---|---|---|
| MD engine | AMBER 24 | README Software Notes |
| Protein force field | **ff19SB** | Pool folder name `H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC` |
| Water model | **OPC** | Pool folder name `H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC` |
| System | H4 histone tail, wild type, 26 residues | `protein.seq`, `assignment.txt` |
| Disorder designation | Residues 1–26 fully disordered | `assignment.txt`: `A 1 26 disordered` |
| Ionic condition | 150 mM Na⁺ | Data files named `H4WT_150Na.dat` / `H4KQ_150Na.dat` |
| Ensemble size | 2000 conformations | `Size_list.txt` contains 2000 data rows |
| Variants compared | WT vs. K-to-Q (charge-neutralized) | README, `SAXSData/` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L22-L25), [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L4), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L30)

The benchmark system is the 26-residue H4 histone tail sequence `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`, assigned as fully disordered — the canonical RANCH input representation of an IDP. The scientific point of running MD rather than random-pool generation is the charge-driven hypothesis: comparing the WT ensemble against the K-to-Q variant, in which lysines are neutralized to glutamine, isolates how electrostatics shape the conformational landscape. The experimental side of this comparison is the pair of SAXS profiles shipped in `SAXSData/` (53 q-points each, three columns: q, I(q), error).

Sources: [Example_tutorial/protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L3), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [README.md](README.md#L5-L13), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L4)

## From Trajectory to Ensemble Pool: The Data Contract

The MD stage terminates by emitting **three artifacts**, and the analysis code binds to them by exact name, column position, and ordering. `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` imports them as: `load([dir,'/Ree_values.mat'])` (exposing variable `R`), `Sizelist = importdata([dir,'/Size_list.txt'])`, then maps `pool.dmax = Sizelist(:,3)`, `pool.rg = Sizelist(:,2)`, and `pool.r = R(1:end)`.

| Artifact | Format | Content | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full-pool structures | PDB/CIF files, numbered by frame | Every saved snapshot, solvent stripped | FFMAKER, GAJOE pool |
| `Size_list.txt` | Whitespace-delimited, 3 columns: `[ID, Rg, Dmax]` (Å) | One row per MD frame, e.g. `1 9.25 26.79` | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` |
| `Ree_values.mat` | MATLAB binary, variable name `R` | End-to-end distance per frame | `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` |
| `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` | GAJOE workfiles, 1 per GA run | Ranked candidate ensembles per generation | `getBestCurve.m` |

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L39), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L30), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_100.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_100.txt#L1-L10)

> [!TIP]
> **Frame numbering is a join key, not a label.** Ensemble member IDs inside `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` index directly into `Size_list.txt` rows and the `Ree_values.mat` ordering — the scripts join `bestcurve(n,1)` against `Sizelist(...)` and `R(...)`. If you re-sort, renumber, or subset the MD frames between the descriptor computation and the GAJOE run, the pool-to-selection mapping silently corrupts and every downstream histogram plots wrong pairings.

One caution inherited from the code comments: the header of `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` instructs *"get end-to-end distance R by running pdb_Rmeas.m in directory with all the PDBs of full pool"* — but `pdb_Rmeas.m` is **not shipped** in this repository. You must compute R<sub>ee</sub> over the full pool with your own tool and persist it as `Ree_values.mat` containing variable `R` before the comparison script can run.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L2-L4), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L39)

## Canonical AMBER Protocol for Pool Generation

Since simulation inputs are not included, the table below states the canonical AMBER sequence for producing a contract-compliant pool. Steps marked *canonical* are standard AMBER practice; the repo-verified anchors are the engine version, force field/water combination, ionic condition, and ensemble size.

| Step | Tool | Purpose | Anchor to repo evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Build system | `tleap` | Load `ff19SB` + OPC water, build the 26-residue sequence, solvate, neutralize/add ions to 150 mM NaCl | ff19SB/OPC folder name; 150 mM Na from data filenames |
| 2. Minimize | `sander`/`pmemd` | Relax solvent and solute geometry | Canonical |
| 3. Heat / equilibrate | `pmemd` | Raise to production temperature, density stabilization (constant-pressure) | Canonical |
| 4. Production | `pmemd` (GPU advisable for 26-residue IDP × multi-µs sampling) | Sample the disordered state; save enough snapshots for a 2000-frame pool | AMBER 24; 2000-row `Size_list.txt` |
| 5. Trajectory post-processing | `cpptraj` | Strip solvent, autoimage, extract per-frame PDB/CIF structures | Full-pool structure files consumed by FFMAKER |
| 6. Descriptor extraction | `cpptraj` (`radial`, distance/max-diameter measurements) | Compute Rg and Dmax per frame → `Size_list.txt`; compute R<sub>ee</sub> per frame → `Ree_values.mat` (variable `R`) | Exact column mapping in `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` |

The pool statistics shipped in the repository give you a sanity target: in `Size_list.txt`, early MD frames show R<sub>g</sub> ≈ 9.2–11.2 Å and D<sub>max</sub> ≈ 27–35 Å for compact states, extending up to R<sub>g</sub> ≈ 18.9 Å and D<sub>max</sub> ≈ 59.8 Å as the ensemble explores extended conformations — a spread wide enough that GAJOE member IDs up to ~1997 appear in the shipped GA workfiles.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L22-L25), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L33-L39), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L30), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_100.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_100.txt#L1-L10)

## MD Pool vs. RANCH Pool: Why MD for Benchmarking

The repository contains two pool-generation paradigms side by side, and understanding the distinction prevents a common misuse: the tutorial under `Example_tutorial/` demonstrates the EOM machinery with 20 **RANCH-generated** random conformations, while the benchmark under `ExampleData/` consumes a 2000-frame **AMBER MD** pool.

| Dimension | RANCH random pool (tutorial) | AMBER MD pool (benchmark) |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling model | Stochastic conformer generation from generic geometry restraints | Force-field-consistent physical sampling (ff19SB/OPC) |
| Typical size | 20 structures (demonstration) | 2000 frames (quantitative) |
| Conformational correlations | None — coordinates sampled independently | Realistic internal correlations from dynamics |
| Role in workflow | Verify the EOM toolchain mechanics | Measure force-field bias against experiment |
| Variants available | Any sequence string | One pool per variant (WT, K-to-Q) per force field |

This distinction is precisely what makes the benchmark meaningful: when GAJOE re-weights the MD pool against experiment, the JSD between the full MD distribution and the selected subset quantifies *how much the SAXS data would need the force field's conformational ensemble to shift*. `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` computes this divergence for both R<sub>g</sub> and R<sub>ee</sub> distributions using binned probability densities and Shannon entropy.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L40), [Example_tutorial/assignment.txt](Example_tutorial/assignment.txt#L1-L2), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L2001), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L225)

## Reading the Shipped MD-Derived Artifacts

The example output in `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/` is the GAJOE result of fitting the **MD pool** against the WT experimental profile, and its header records the benchmark-scale settings actually used: `CYCLE: 29 Chi^2: 1.226 GENER.:1000 ENSEMBLES: 50 CURVES: 9` — that is, 1000 GA generations, 50 candidate ensembles per generation, 9 curves per ensemble, with the best fit achieved at cycle 29. This is an order of magnitude heavier than the tutorial's quick-run parameters, and it is the scale you should reproduce for quantitative comparisons.

Sources: [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/profiles_001_1.fit#L1-L1), [README.md](README.md#L30-L40)

Selection provenance flows through `GA_CYCLE_1.txt` … `GA_CYCLE_100.txt` (one file per GA run, enabled via GAJOE's *"Save workfiles with the entire GA runs?"* option). `getBestCurve.m` parses all 100 workfiles, tallies how often each pool-structure ID was selected, and returns the `[PDBnum, freq]` best-curve matrix; `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` then renders the 2D R<sub>g</sub>–R<sub>ee</sub> and R<sub>g</sub>–D<sub>max</sub> comparison of **full MD pool vs. EOM subset**, prints mean ± standard error for both ensembles, and computes the Jensen–Shannon divergence. The companion script `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` closes the loop by plotting the EOM ensemble fit against `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat` in direct, Kratky, and residual forms.

Sources: [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L10-L43), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L14-L18), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L73-L130), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L225), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L7-L14)

> [!TIP]
> **Reproduce the benchmark GAJOE settings before drawing conclusions.** The shipped example used GENER 1000 / ENSEMBLES 50 / CURVES 9 with workfile saving enabled (`nRuns = 100`, `curvesPerEnsemble` set in the MATLAB parameters block). The tutorial's 100-generation, 20-conformation demo exists only to verify the toolchain — its JSD values are not meaningful.

## Continue the Journey

A logical reading path through the catalog: ground the system context in [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study), study the EOM machinery this page feeds into — [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation), [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles), and [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting) — then master the descriptors the MD stage exports in [Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree](16-structural-descriptors-rg-dmax-ree). For the consumption side, proceed to [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles), [2D Ensemble Comparison Histograms](11-2d-ensemble-comparison-histograms), [Jensen-Shannon Divergence Quantification](12-jensen-shannon-divergence-quantification), and [SAXS Fit, Kratky Plot, and Residuals](13-saxs-fit-kratky-plot-and-residuals). Finally, apply the same MD-to-EOM contract to your own system via [Extending Workflow to Other IDPs](19-extending-workflow-to-other-idps), with installation prerequisites covered in [Software Requirements and Installation](3-software-requirements-and-installation).


# Extending Workflow to Other IDPs



The H4 histone tail benchmark is not a sequence-locked pipeline — it is a **template**. Every script in this repository consumes GAJOE outputs and plain-text inputs through path variables and a single "User-defined parameters" block; no script hardcodes the H4 sequence. Porting the MD–SAXS ensemble workflow to another intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) therefore reduces to swapping a **small, well-defined adaptation surface**: two RANCH sequence files, one experimental SAXS profile, one conformational pool, and a handful of axis-scale parameters. This page walks through that adaptation end-to-end for advanced users, assuming you have already run the H4 case once — if not, start with [EOM Tutorial with ATSAS Tools](4-eom-tutorial-with-atsas-tools) and [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).

![H4SAXSMDgraphic](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/328c5a72-924c-43e9-93a6-d43f74d66d93)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L18), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L27), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L22)

## Portability Map: What Changes and What Doesn't

From first principles, the pipeline has two layers. The **invariant core** — `getBestCurve.m`, the JSD computation, the plotting logic in both MATLAB and Python — operates purely on GAJOE output formats (`GA_CYCLE_*.txt`, `Size_list.txt`, `profiles_*.fit`, distribution files) and never sees your sequence. The **adaptation surface** is the set of inputs that encode *which* IDP you are studying. The repository itself proves this modularity: `SAXSData/` ships two experimental profiles (WT and K-to-Q charge-neutralized H4) that are analyzed with identical scripts and identical pool machinery — only the `.dat` path and plot color change between them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph proteinSpecific["Protein-specific inputs"]
        S["protein.seq<br/>+ assignment.txt"]
        P["MD pool PDBs<br/>(AMBER, ff19SB/OPC)"]
        X["Experimental SAXS .dat"]
    end
    subgraph invariant["Invariant tooling"]
        R["RANCH"] --> F["FFMAKER"]
        F --> G["GAJOE"]
        M["MATLAB scripts"] 
        PY["Python scripts"]
    end
    S --> R
    P --> F
    R --> F
    F --> G
    X --> G
    G --> M
    G --> PY
```

| Pipeline stage | Files involved | Protein-specific? |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence definition | `protein.seq`, `assignment.txt` | **Yes — swap entirely** |
| Conformational pool | AMBER MD trajectories or RANCH CIFs | **Yes — regenerate** |
| Experimental data | `SAXSData/<protein>_<salt>.dat` | **Yes — supply yours** |
| Theoretical profiles | FFMAKER `intensities_*.csv`, `size_statistics_*.csv` | No — regenerated automatically |
| GA fitting | GAJOE output directory (`GA001/curve_1/…`) | No — paths only |
| Ensemble analysis | `getBestCurve.m`, `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m`, `plotEOMSAXScomparison.m` | No — parameter block only |
| Plotting | `graph.py`, `2d.py` | No — two path constants |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L18), [README.md](README.md#L34-L36), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L19-L39), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L5), [SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat#L1-L6)

## Step 1: Encode the New IDP Sequence for RANCH

RANCH consumes exactly two files, both present in `Example_tutorial/`. The `protein.seq` file is a minimal FASTA: a one-line chain header (`>A`) followed by the one-letter sequence — for H4 that is the 26-residue tail `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI`. The companion `assignment.txt` is a single row with four whitespace-separated fields: chain ID, first residue index, last residue index, and the secondary-structure class `disordered`, which instructs RANCH to generate random-coil-like conformers for the whole chain. To extend the workflow, replace both files with your target's sequence and make the residue range in `assignment.txt` match the sequence length exactly (26 → *N* for your IDP).

| File | H4 tail (shipped) | Generic IDP (your target) |
|---|---|---|
| `protein.seq` line 1 | `>A` | `>X` (your chain ID) |
| `protein.seq` line 2 | `SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKVLRDNI` | your sequence, one-letter code |
| `assignment.txt` | `A 1 26 disordered` | `X 1 N disordered` |

Keep the header chain ID consistent between the two files — RANCH matches the `assignment.txt` chain letter against the `protein.seq` header. If your IDP contains ordered domains flanking the disordered region, add a row per segment and use the appropriate class tag per ATSAS conventions instead of a single `disordered` row.

Sources: [protein.seq](Example_tutorial/protein.seq#L1-L2), [assignment.txt](assignment.txt#L1), [README.md](README.md#L38-L47), [RANCH Conformational Pool Generation](6-ranch-conformational-pool-generation)

## Step 2: Supply the Conformational Pool and Experimental Profile

Two inputs replace the H4 defaults here. First, the conformational pool: either let RANCH generate it from your new sequence files (the `--repetitions` flag controls pool size), or — as the H4 production data did — generate structures from your own AMBER 24 trajectory using ff19SB with OPC water, then feed those PDBs directly into FFMAKER in place of `pool_20/*.cif` (the README explicitly supports this substitution). Pool-generation specifics for AMBER are covered in [MD Ensemble Generation with AMBER](18-md-ensemble-generation-with-amber). Second, the experimental SAXS profile: the parsers in this repo expect a three-column `Q, I(Q), Error` file with **four header lines**, exactly the format of the shipped `H4WT_150Na.dat` and `H4KQ_150Na.dat` (whose only meaningful differences are the point count `# 53` vs `# 56` in the header comment and the intensity scale). Both MATLAB and Python readers tolerate header variation — see Step 5 — but the MATLAB reader's header count is fixed, so normalize your instrument export to this shape.

> [!TIP]
> The end-to-end distance matrix `Ree_values.mat` (workspace variable `R`) is **not produced by any script in this repository** — `make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m` documents that it comes from running the external `pdb_Rmeas.m` utility over your full pool PDBs. For a new IDP you must regenerate this file for the new pool, or the 2D histograms and JSD calculation will fail at the `load()` step.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L49-L60), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L3-L4), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L35-L39), [SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat#L1-L4), [SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat](SAXSData/H4KQ_150Na.dat#L1-L4), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16)

## Step 3: Re-run the RANCH → FFMAKER → GAJOE Chain

The three ATSAS commands are identical in form to the tutorial; only pool-size-derived numbers change. The tutorial's demonstration values (20 conformations, 100 generations) are intentionally minimal — the shipped production data used a ~2000-conformation pool and 1000 generations, visible in `GA_CYCLE_1.txt` reaching generation 1000. Scale `--repetitions`, `--generation`, and `--ensemble` to your IDP's conformational complexity, and keep the GAJOE prompt **"Save workfiles with the entire GA runs? (default: no)"** answered `y`.

```bash
ranch --repetitions N --prefix pool_N/model_ --seed 12345 assignment.txt protein.seq
ffmaker --output intensities_N.csv --pool size_statistics_N.csv pool_N/*.cif
gajoe --intensity intensities_N.csv --size size_statistics_N.csv \
      --times T --generation G --ensemble E --minimum 1 --maximum M \
      --no-repeated  <your_protein>_<salt>.dat
```

| GAJOE setting | H4 tutorial value | Adaptation rule for a new IDP |
|---|---|---|
| `--repetitions` (pool size) | 20 | Scale with conformational complexity; production H4 used ~2000 |
| `--times` (independent GA runs) | 1 | Increase for quantitative work; must equal MATLAB `nRuns` |
| `--generation` | 100 | Production example converged at 1000 generations |
| `--ensemble` (candidates/generation) | 20 | Match pool size (ATSAS caps pool at 2000) |
| `--minimum` / `--maximum` | 1 / 10 | `--maximum` must equal MATLAB `curvesPerEnsemble` (max 50) |
| `--no-repeated` | set | Retain unless duplicate conformers are physically meaningful |
| Experimental `.dat` | `H4WT_150Na.dat` | Your file, 3-column, 4 header lines |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L89), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_1.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/GA_CYCLE_1.txt#L19999-L20001), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L8-L9), [GAJOE Genetic Algorithm Ensemble Fitting](8-gajoe-genetic-algorithm-ensemble-fitting), [FFMAKER Theoretical SAXS Profiles](7-ffmaker-theoretical-saxs-profiles)

## Step 4: Retune the MATLAB "User-defined Parameters" Block

Both analysis scripts are driven entirely by their first code block — per the README, "mostly the paths just need to be matched," but for a new IDP the **axis limits also require rescaling** because they encode H4's physical size (its pool spans Rg ≈ 9–10 Å, Dmax ≈ 27–31 Å, as seen in `Size_list.txt`, while the plots reserve `[5 30]` × `[20 80]` × `[0 80]`). A 100-residue IDP will clip silently at these limits. `getBestCurve` is parameterless from your perspective — it inherits `nRuns` and `curvesPerEnsemble` from the calling script, and its parser (delimiter `-`, last *k* rows per `GA_CYCLE` file) works for any IDP.

| MATLAB variable | Location | H4 value | Adaptation for new IDP |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dir` / `folder` | `make2Dplot…` L14 / `plotEOMSAXS…` L9 | `ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1` | Your `GA00X/curve_Y` path |
| `nRuns` | `make2Dplot…` L15 | 100 | = GAJOE `--times`; = number of `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files |
| `curvesPerEnsemble` | `make2Dplot…` L16 | 20 | = GAJOE `--maximum` (1–50) |
| `xlim_Dmax`, `ylim_Rg`, `xlim_R` | `make2Dplot…` L18 | `[20 80]`, `[5 30]`, `[0 80]` | Rescale to your IDP's size distributions |
| `binsRg`, `binsDmax`, `binsR`, `gajoeHistBins` | `make2Dplot…` L21-L26 | 22, 22, 22, 15 | Adjust for distribution resolution |
| `expData` | `plotEOMSAXS…` L15 | `SAXSData/H4WT_150Na.dat`, 4 header lines | Your `.dat`; keep `NumHeaderLines=4` accurate |
| `fitFile` | `plotEOMSAXS…` L16 | `profiles_001_1.fit`, 1 header line | Update filename for your run |
| `theColour` | `plotEOMSAXS…` L12-L13 | `[238 68 0]` (WT) / `[46 80 122]` (KQ) | Optional per-variant color |

> [!TIP]
> The coupling between GAJOE and MATLAB is silent and two-fold: `nRuns` ↔ "number of times the genetic algorithm is repeated" and `curvesPerEnsemble` ↔ "maximum number of curves per ensemble" *at GAJOE runtime*. Additionally, GAJOE defaults to **not** saving workfiles — without answering `y` at that prompt, no `GA_CYCLE_*.txt` files exist and `getBestCurve` has nothing to parse.

Sources: [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L13-L27), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L36-L39), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L8-L22), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L19-L27), [ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt](ExampleData/H4_tail_WT_ff19SB_OPC/GA001/curve_1/Size_list.txt#L1-L10), [Best-Curve Reconstruction from GA Cycles](10-best-curve-reconstruction-from-ga-cycles)

## Step 5: Point the Python Scripts at Your Output

The tutorial plotting scripts carry three path constants in total, and nothing else is protein-aware. In `graph.py`, the single constant `folder = Path("GA001/curve_1")` locates the `.fit` profile (globbed via `profiles_*.fit`) and the `Rg`/`Dmax`/`Ree` distribution files. In `2d.py`, update `size_file` to your FFMAKER `size_statistics_*.csv` and `selected_dir` to your `GA00X/curve_Y/pdbs` folder; the script cross-checks GAJOE-selected structure names against the pool CSV and raises an assertion if any selected structure is missing, which doubles as a free consistency audit after you swap pools. `graph.py`'s numeric parser skips every non-numeric line, so the multi-line headers of ATSAS distribution files (`Rg`, pool/ensemble averages) are tolerated automatically regardless of protein.

| Script | Constant | H4 default | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `graph.py` | `folder` | `GA001/curve_1` | Point at your GAJOE output directory |
| `2d.py` | `size_file` | `size_statistics_20.csv` | Your FFMAKER size statistics CSV |
| `2d.py` | `selected_dir` | `GA001/curve_1/pdbs` | Your run's `pdbs/` folder (CIF or PDB) |

Sources: [graph.py](graph.py#L5-L24), [graph.py](graph.py#L40-L44), [2d.py](2d.py#L8-L9), [2d.py](2d.py#L28-L41), [SAXS Curve and Distribution Plots](14-saxs-curve-and-distribution-plots), [Rg-Ree Scatter Plot with Marginals](15-rg-ree-scatter-plot-with-marginals)

## Adaptation Workflow at a Glance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Write protein.seq + assignment.txt<br/>for target IDP"] --> B{"Pool source?"}
    B -->|"RANCH random pool"| C["ranch --repetitions N"]
    B -->|"MD ensemble"| D["AMBER ff19SB/OPC trajectory<br/>+ pdb_Rmeas.m over full pool"]
    C --> E["ffmaker: intensities + size_statistics"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["gajoe with your .dat<br/>save workfiles: y"]
    F --> G["Edit MATLAB User-defined parameters<br/>paths + nRuns + curvesPerEnsemble + axis limits"]
    G --> H["make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m<br/>plotEOMSAXScomparison.m"]
    H --> I["Edit Python path constants<br/>graph.py + 2d.py"]
    I --> J{"Consistency checks pass?"}
    J -->|"yes"| K["Interpret: JSD, Rg/Dmax/Ree shifts"]
    J -->|"no"| L["Troubleshooting table below"]
    L --> G
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L30-L118), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L185-L206)

## Verification Checklist and Troubleshooting

Before trusting any cross-protein comparison, verify the adapter surface explicitly. The failure modes below are all deterministic consequences of the parsers examined above — none involve the algorithmic core.

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `getBestCurve` returns empty / MATLAB errors on `GA_CYCLE` | GAJOE "Save workfiles with entire GA runs?" left at default `no` | Re-run GAJOE answering `y`; files `GA_CYCLE_1.txt`… appear under `curve_N` |
| `Unable to read file 'Ree_values.mat'` | Variable `R` never regenerated for new pool | Run `pdb_Rmeas.m` over full-pool PDBs; save result as `Ree_values.mat` |
| 2D plots show clipped/empty point clouds | H4-scale axis limits (`[5 30]` Rg etc.) kept for larger IDP | Rescale `xlim_Dmax`, `ylim_Rg`, `xlim_R` from your `Size_list.txt` ranges |
| MATLAB misreads experimental curve | Header-line count ≠ 4 in your instrument export | Reformat to 3 columns + 4 header lines, or adjust `NumHeaderLines` |
| `graph.py` silently plots no distributions | Glob patterns expect `*_distr_*.dat`; some ATSAS builds write `.txt` | Edit the three patterns at L41–L43 to match your GAJOE's actual extensions |
| `2d.py` assertion "Some selected structures were not found in the pool!" | `size_statistics` CSV and `pdbs/` folder from different runs/pools | Regenerate both from the same FFMAKER/GAJOE run |
| GA rejects pool / poor fits with tiny pool | Tutorial-scale pool (20) used for quantitative claim | Increase pool size; README warns demonstration settings are non-quantitative |

Sources: [graph.py](graph.py#L40-L44), [2d.py](2d.py#L40-L41), [getBestCurve.m](getBestCurve.m#L8-L9), [make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m](make2Dplot_fromEOMresults.m#L18-L26), [README.md](README.md#L89-L118), [plotEOMSAXScomparison.m](plotEOMSAXScomparison.m#L15-L16)

## What Survives the Port Untouched

Everything downstream of the GAJOE output directory is protein-agnostic: best-curve reconstruction tallies structure IDs across GA cycles with a categorical tabulation; the Jensen–Shannon divergence compares MD-pool vs EOM-selected histograms in bins you define; and the Kratky/residual plots are pure *q*-space arithmetic. Because the two shipped SAXS datasets (WT and KQ) already exercise the "same machinery, different data" path, a successful H4 run is your regression baseline: after swapping in a new IDP, re-running the H4 configuration should reproduce the shipped `ExampleData` results bit-for-bit, confirming your environment before you trust new-protein output. For the analytical interpretation of the quantities you just regenerated — Rg, Dmax, Ree and their ensemble meaning — proceed to [Structural Descriptors: Rg, Dmax, Ree](16-structural-descriptors-rg-dmax-ree), and for a worked production example of the full chain, [H4 Histone Tail Case Study](17-h4-histone-tail-case-study).
